passages.title: Predictions, loss, gradients, and weight updates: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes A gradient is local. It describes the slope at the current weights, not where the best weights are, and real loss surfaces have many dips and flat regions. A falling training loss shows that the model fits its training batches better; it does not show that it predicts new examples well. In PyTorch, gradients add up across backward passes until they are cleared, so a training loop that forgets optimizer.zero_grad() updates with stale, summed gradients. Key takeaways - The loss is one number that measures how wrong the predictions are on a batch. - The gradient gives the direction and steepness of the loss for each weight. The update moves each weight a learning-rate-sized step against it. - Too large a learning rate can make the weights swing past the minimum; too small a rate makes progress slow. Compare rates on held-out data. References Official references checked October 20, 2026. - PyTorch: automatic differentiation with torch.autograd - PyTorch: optimizing model parameters (epochs, batch size, learning rate) - PyTorch 2.14: torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss - PyTorch 2.14: torch.optim.SGD

passages.title: Messages, prompts, and context windows: What the model receives with each request
passages.text: A chat application usually represents a conversation as messages. Each message has content and a role, such as user or assistant. A system message can supply application instructions. Supported roles and their treatment depend on the model and serving interface. A prompt is input supplied to guide a model's output. In chat systems, that input can include instructions, earlier messages, retrieved documents, and the current question. A chat template formats structured messages into the sequence expected by a particular model. The context window is the amount of sequence context supported for a request under a particular model and runtime configuration. For generation, the application must account for input and the intended output allowance. A published model maximum and a runtime's configured limit need not be identical. Consider a customer asking, “Can you explain that?” The current message alone does not identify “that.” If the application sends the preceding delivery-policy discussion, the model has relevant context. If it omits those messages, the application has changed the information available to the model. An ordinary chat request does not make every earlier interaction available automatically. Some hosted services store conversation state; other interfaces expect the caller to resend it. Check the interface contract. Application memory and runtime caching are different responsibilities.

passages.title: Messages, prompts, and context windows: What the model receives with each request
passages.text: When a conversation becomes too large, the application needs a policy: reject, select relevant turns, summarize, or otherwise reduce context. Removing arbitrary text can delete the user's current question or separate a tool result from its request. The later context-budget build makes that policy explicit and tests what is retained.

passages.title: Messages, prompts, and context windows: From conversation history to a new reply
passages.text: Conversation data is what the application chooses to send: the system instructions, the earlier delivery-policy turns and the current question, “Can you explain that?”. Chat formatting renders those messages with the selected model's chat template. The result is a bounded request: the formatted input must fit the context window and still leave room for the reply. Notice that the application decides what enters the first box. A turn it leaves out never reaches the model.

passages.title: Messages, prompts, and context windows: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Compose a two-turn conversation in a text editor in which the second question uses “that.” Read only the second question, then read both turns. Identify the information the first turn provides and why the second question needs it. Check your understanding

passages.title: Messages, prompts, and context windows: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes A longer context window does not make the model use every supplied fact correctly. Untrusted documents are data and must not gain permission to override application policy. Key takeaways - Messages are structured application data; a chat template turns them into model input. - The model receives only what the request supplies. Check whether the interface stores history or expects the caller to resend it. - Context selection is an application decision with failure cases. Best practices - Preserve required instructions and the current user request. - Count the actual formatted conversation and reserve output space. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - Hugging Face: chat templates - Ollama: chat message and generation fields

passages.title: Foundation, frontier, base, and instruction-tuned models: Model labels describe different properties
passages.text: A model can have several descriptions at once. Calling something “frontier” does not tell you whether its weights are available. Calling it “instruction-tuned” does not tell you how much memory it needs. A foundation model is broadly trained for adaptation across multiple tasks. A base language model typically refers to a pretrained model before subsequent instruction-oriented adaptation. An instruction-tuned model has undergone training intended to improve following instructions. The exact development process belongs in its documentation. Frontier generally describes highly advanced capabilities relative to contemporary models, with definitions varying by context. It is a moving capability description. It is not a license or a requirement for building useful applications. LLM means large language model; SLM means small language model. There is no universal parameter threshold that turns every small model into a large one. Size descriptions help with initial expectations but do not replace measurement on the task and hardware. A reasoning model is often trained or configured to spend additional computation on intermediate problem solving. A visible explanation is not proof of correctness, and a longer answer is not by itself evidence of stronger reasoning. A mixture of experts (MoE) architecture conditionally activates parts of a model; its total parameter count and active computation describe different things.

passages.title: Foundation, frontier, base, and instruction-tuned models: Model labels describe different properties
passages.text: For our support inbox, these labels are search clues. We still need evidence that a release can classify the relevant messages, follow the required format, and run within the available resources. We do not choose it merely because one label sounds more advanced.

passages.title: Foundation, frontier, base, and instruction-tuned models: Compare training, capability and access
passages.text: Each box is a separate way to describe the same release. Purpose and training says what adaptation the model has had, such as base or instruction-tuned. Capability and structure covers labels such as frontier, small or large, and dense or MoE; a dense model uses all of its parameters for every input. Access and license must be checked on their own for that release. One release has a value on every axis. A label on one axis tells you nothing certain about the others.

passages.title: Foundation, frontier, base, and instruction-tuned models: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Provider names, family names, and capability labels cannot substitute for exact release documentation. A small model can suit a narrow task; a more capable general model can still fail your required output contract. Key takeaways - Model descriptions answer different questions and can overlap. - Capability labels alone do not tell you access permissions or task suitability. - To choose between releases, compare them on your own task with a fixed set of check messages. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - UK government: a stated frontier AI definition - Hugging Face: model-card metadata and base models

passages.title: Models, runtimes, and hardware: Model files need software and working memory
passages.text: A model file sitting on disk is not a running service. A runtime is software that executes compatible model computations. A server accepts requests and coordinates that execution. One program may package these responsibilities together, but the responsibilities remain useful to distinguish. To run the inbox model, the system loads the required weights and configuration, prepares input, executes computation, and returns output. Input preparation may need tokenizer files. Not every file format or model architecture is supported by every runtime. The CPU is the computer's general-purpose processor. A GPU is hardware well suited to many parallel numerical operations. RAM is working memory; a dedicated GPU may also have its own memory, often called VRAM. Unified-memory machines have a different physical arrangement. Storage capacity and working-memory capacity answer different questions. Precision describes how numerical values are represented. Quantization uses lower-precision representations for some values. It can reduce storage or memory requirements, but compatibility, speed and output quality must be evaluated for the actual configuration. Memory is needed for more than the downloaded weights: intermediate computations, runtime buffers, concurrent requests, and generation state also matter. A KV cache stores attention-related state that a runtime can reuse during generation. Longer sequences and more active requests can increase that state. It is not the customer's long-term memory store.

passages.title: Models, runtimes, and hardware: Model files need software and working memory
passages.text: You do not need a GPU to read these lessons. When a build runs a model, it states the hardware it was tested on and keeps measurements separate from estimates; the request-tracer build, for example, records its machine, memory and software versions.

passages.title: Models, runtimes, and hardware: Files, runtime and hardware work together
passages.text: The three boxes are separate requirements, not steps in a sequence. Files on storage are what you download: weights, configuration and tokenizer assets. The runtime in memory prepares inputs and executes the computation, and it must support those files. Hardware supplies the processors and the working memory the workload needs. A local run needs all three. Notice that the first box tells you how much storage the files use, not how much working memory the runtime will need.

passages.title: Models, runtimes, and hardware: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Inspect your computer’s reported processor, memory and free storage. Keep these as separate fields. Now list what additional evidence you would need before claiming that a particular model runs well on it. Check your understanding

passages.title: Models, runtimes, and hardware: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Quantization does not guarantee faster execution on every device. A model that fits in memory can still respond too slowly or miss the quality requirement. Key takeaways - Artifacts, runtime, server, and hardware are distinct components. - Working memory holds more than the weights, so download size is not the full memory requirement. - Memory and performance depend on the complete workload, including sequence length and concurrent requests. Best practices - Report exact precision, runtime, context and hardware with measurements. - Begin with one small request before increasing concurrency. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - Ollama: model execution API overview - Hugging Face: KV-cache strategies - PyTorch: tensors and devices

passages.title: How does a language model generate text?: Predicting the next token
passages.text: Many language models generate text one token at a time. Such a model is called an autoregressive language model: each new token is predicted from the tokens before it, including the tokens it has just generated. Given the tokens so far, the model computes scores for possible next tokens. A selection procedure chooses one, appends it to the sequence, and the model predicts again. The model's raw output scores are often called logits. A generation procedure can turn those scores into probabilities and choose among candidates. Sampling means selecting according to a probability distribution rather than always taking the highest-scoring candidate. The lesson “Output limits, sampling, and streaming” covers these controls. Follow one support-inbox reply. A customer writes, “Where is my parcel?” The application asks a model to draft a reply, and the draft so far reads “Your parcel is”. This is a teaching example, not a captured model response:

passages.title: How does a language model generate text?: Predicting the next token
passages.text: 1. The model computes a score for every token in its vocabulary. Candidates that could follow “Your parcel is” include pieces such as delayed, on and arriving. We show no scores because none were measured. 2. The selection procedure chooses one candidate, here delayed. 3. The application appends it. The context is now “Your parcel is delayed”. 4. The model computes new scores from this longer context. A period may now be likely, and after it a stop token can end the reply. Each selected token becomes part of the input for the next prediction. If step 2 had chosen arriving, every later prediction would condition on a different sequence. Next-token prediction explains how the text was produced, not whether it is true. “Your parcel is delayed” can be a likely continuation even when the parcel arrived yesterday. The actual status of a customer's order requires a current, authorized data source. Model documentation often mentions attention, a mechanism for combining information from positions in the input sequence, and the transformer, which arranges attention with other neural-network components. They determine how the scores are computed. You can follow the generation loop without those details.

passages.title: How does a language model generate text?: Predicting the next token
passages.text: Generating a convincing support reply is one step in an application. The application still needs to provide relevant facts, inspect results, and decide whether a person should review them.

passages.title: How does a language model generate text?: How the generation loop repeats
passages.text: Start at Current context, which holds “Your parcel is”. The model uses that context and its learned weights to predict possible next tokens, and the generation settings select one token. Append the selected token makes the context one token longer, and the return path sends that longer context back to the top. The loop leaves only when a stop condition is met, such as a stop token or a configured output limit. Notice that no box in the loop consults a tracking record.

passages.title: How does a language model generate text?: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Think of two possible continuations of “Your parcel is”. Then add “The tracking record says it arrived yesterday” before the phrase. Explain how adding evidence should affect the desired answer. Check your understanding

passages.title: How does a language model generate text?: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Not every model is an autoregressive text generator. A runtime, the software that executes the model's computations, can also optimize how it carries out generation internally. This lesson describes a useful conceptual loop, not a complete implementation trace. Key takeaways - Generation repeats one step: score candidate tokens, select one, append it, and predict again from the longer context. - Plausible text and verified application facts require different checks. Best practices - In a drafted reply, mark each statement that depends on current data, such as an order status or a date, and supply that data from an authorized source. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - Hugging Face: text generation - Hugging Face: generation strategies

passages.title: Protocols, JSON-RPC, clients, servers, and discovery: A protocol fixes the messages two programs exchange
passages.text: The order tools from the first lesson now live in a separate program, written by another team. Later the assistant may also hand shipping questions to an agent run by another company. Without an agreed message format, every pair of programs needs its own glue code. A protocol is a written agreement about which messages exist, what they contain, in what order they are sent and what they mean. A client sends requests and a server answers them. These are roles, not machines. In the HTTP lesson, the client and the server both ran on your own computer. JSON-RPC 2.0 is a small message format. MCP uses it, and A2A offers it as one of three bindings. A request has "jsonrpc": "2.0", a method name, optional params and an id. The response repeats that id and contains either a result or an error, never both. A notification is a request without an id; the receiver sends no response. JSON-RPC does not care how the bytes travel, which is why one format can run over standard input and output or over HTTP.

passages.title: Protocols, JSON-RPC, clients, servers, and discovery: A protocol fixes the messages two programs exchange
passages.text: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, connects an AI application to servers that provide tools, resources and prompts. The application is the host; it creates one client for each server it connects to. This lesson uses MCP specification version 2026-07-28, in which the protocol is stateless: every request carries its protocol version and the client's capabilities in a _meta field, and a server must not rely on earlier requests on the same connection. Versions up to 2025-11-25 opened each session with an initialize handshake instead, so older guides show that step. MCP defines two standard transports. With stdio, the client starts the server as a subprocess and they exchange newline-delimited messages. With Streamable HTTP, each message is an HTTP POST to one MCP endpoint, and the reply comes back as JSON or as a stream. Discovery is how a client learns what a server offers before using it. In MCP, server/discover returns the protocol versions, capabilities and identity the server reports, and tools/list returns its tool definitions. A2A, the Agent2Agent protocol, connects a client agent to a remote agent that works on tasks. Its discovery document is the Agent Card, a JSON file that lists the agent's identity, endpoint, skills and authentication requirements. One discovery method serves it at https://{domain}/.well-known/agent-card.json; registries and direct configuration are others.

passages.title: Protocols, JSON-RPC, clients, servers, and discovery: A protocol fixes the messages two programs exchange
passages.text: Discovery describes a server; it does not vouch for it. MCP says the server's self-reported name is not verified and should not drive security decisions. The A2A specification says clients should verify at least one signature on an Agent Card before trusting it.

passages.title: Protocols, JSON-RPC, clients, servers, and discovery: Trace one discovery and one tool call over MCP
passages.text: Read the figure from the top, one pair at a time. In pair 1 the client sends server/discover. The result lists supportedVersions and the server's capabilities, such as whether it offers tools at all. This step is optional: a client can send any request directly and handle a version error if one comes back. In pair 2 the client sends tools/list and receives tool definitions, each with a name, a description and an inputSchema. The host passes those definitions to the model. In pair 3, after the model proposes a call and the host's own checks pass, the client sends tools/call. The result carries content and an isError flag. Every result points back to the request with the same id. That pairing lets a client send several requests and still match each answer to its question.

passages.title: Protocols, JSON-RPC, clients, servers, and discovery: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: A client receives three messages from an MCP server. For each, decide what kind of message it is and who should act on it. 1. A response with "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"} to a request whose method was tools/run. 2. A response with a result that contains "isError": true and the text “Order not found.” 3. A message with "method": "notifications/tools/list_changed", no id, and a subscriptionId in its _meta. Check your understanding

passages.title: Protocols, JSON-RPC, clients, servers, and discovery: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes A protocol makes programs interoperable; it does not make them trustworthy. A server that follows MCP exactly can still return false data or offer a harmful tool. Protocol versions change, and examples written for one version can fail against another. Check which version a server and an SDK support before you copy an example. A tool definition from tools/list is input to your application, not a rule your application must obey. Decide in your own code which listed tools a model may see at all. Key takeaways - JSON-RPC pairs each request with one result or error through the id. A notification has no id and gets no response. - MCP connects a host's clients to servers of tools, resources and prompts. In version 2026-07-28 each request carries its own version and capabilities. - Discovery, through MCP server/discover or an A2A Agent Card, tells a client what a server reports about itself. Trust still needs its own checks. References Official references checked October 20, 2026, against MCP specification version 2026-07-28 and A2A specification version 1.0. - JSON-RPC 2.0 specification - MCP: architecture overview - MCP specification: base protocol and statelessness - MCP specification: discovery - MCP specification: transports - A2A specification: agent discovery and bindings - A2A: A2A and MCP

passages.title: Python values, collections, functions, and errors: Turn input into a valid message
passages.text: A support inbox receives questions as text. Before a later build sends a question anywhere, the program must check that the question is usable text and put it into one consistent message format. This lesson reads the small function that does that, make_message. First, you need names for the kinds of values it handles. A string is text, written between quotes. A number can represent a count or measurement. A boolean is a true/false value. None represents the absence of a value. The type matters: the text “3” and the number 3 are different inputs. A list holds an ordered sequence of values. A dictionary associates keys with values. Our message is a dictionary with the keys role and content. A conversation can be a list of such dictionaries. A variable is a name used to refer to a value. A function groups instructions so you can call them with different inputs. make_message(content) is a function: it checks the content and returns a message dictionary. Return supplies the function result to its caller. The if statement chooses what to execute based on a condition. In our function, the condition rejects an input that is not a string or has no non-whitespace characters. strip() returns text without surrounding whitespace. The function then constructs a normalized message.

passages.title: Python values, collections, functions, and errors: Turn input into a valid message
passages.text: An exception reports an error that interrupts ordinary control flow. ValueError indicates an unacceptable value in this example. passages.title: Python values, collections, functions, and errors: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes This validator only enforces a small input contract. It does not detect every harmful instruction, establish authorization, or make a complete model request safe. Key takeaways - Types and containers define the shape of application data. - Functions should state what they accept, return, and reject. - An explicit exception reports bad input; silently replacing it would hide the problem. Best practices - Validate inputs at application boundaries. - Catch specific expected errors; keep unexpected failures visible for investigation. passages.title: Retrieval, context assembly, citations, and RAG: Give the model evidence it can cite
passages.text: You want an assistant to answer “” from your own six study notes, not from whatever its model weights happen to contain. The model has never seen your notes. The application must find the right notes, give them to the model with the question, and then check that the answer uses them. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is that arrangement. A retriever, such as the BM25 or embedding search from the earlier lessons, selects passages from a collection. A language model then generates an answer from a request that contains those passages. The original RAG paper by Lewis and colleagues (NeurIPS 2020) paired a neural retriever over a vector index with a generator that conditions on the retrieved passages. The idea is the same with any retriever. Context assembly is the step between retrieval and generation. The application chooses which retrieved passages to include, in which order, and how to label them. It must fit them into a budget: the space left in the model's context window after the instruction, the question and room for the answer. The lesson Messages, prompts, and context windows explains the context window.

passages.title: Retrieval, context assembly, citations, and RAG: Give the model evidence it can cite
passages.text: A citation is a label in the answer, such as [n1], that points to one supplied passage. An answer is grounded when every claim is supported by a passage the model received. A citation makes a claim checkable. It does not make the claim true.

passages.title: Retrieval, context assembly, citations, and RAG: Retrieve, assemble a labeled context, then check the citations
passages.text: The first box is the question. The second box retrieves the three highest BM25 scores from the six notes. Only notes match any question term, so all three are kept for assembly. The third box is where retrieval quality becomes context quality. The assembler walks down the ranking and keeps each passage whose words fit the -word budget. It keeps n1 ( words) and n5 ( words), then drops n6 because it . Note n5, about context windows, ranked second only because it contains the word how. A weak match used budget that the next-ranked note could have used. The fourth box sends the assembled text below to a language model. This lesson does not run a model, so the next step uses hand-written drafts in place of model output. The fifth box checks citations. For each label in a draft, it asks one question: was a passage with this label in the context? That check is mechanical and cheap. Notice what it does not ask: whether the passage says what the claim says.

Draft Text a b c d To reproduce the trace, download context_trace.py and run it with Python 3.10 or newer. Compare its output with the recorded trace. Check your understanding

passages.title: Retrieval, context assembly, citations, and RAG: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes A retrieved note can contain text written as an instruction, such as “ignore the earlier rules.” The OWASP project for generative AI security calls this indirect prompt injection, and it states that RAG does not fully prevent it. This lesson counts words to keep the arithmetic visible. A model's context window is measured in tokens. Count the assembled request with the tokenizer of the model you call, as the lesson What are tokens and tokenizers? explains. The instruction tells the model to say when the sources do not answer the question. A model can still ignore that instruction. Check for answers that make claims when retrieval returned nothing useful. Key takeaways - RAG adds retrieved passages to the model request. Retrieval errors become context errors, because the model sees only what the assembler kept. - Context assembly chooses, orders and labels passages within a budget. A weak match can use budget that the next-ranked passage needed. - A citation check confirms that each label names a supplied passage. It does not confirm that the passage supports the claim. References Official references checked October 20, 2026. - Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (arXiv 2005.11401) - OWASP GenAI Security Project: LLM01 Prompt Injection

passages.title: Read a model card and check its license: Find evidence about a specific release
passages.text: A model card is documentation supplied with a model. On Hugging Face it commonly appears as the repository's README with structured metadata. It can describe intended tasks, training, evaluation, limitations, and how to run the release. For our support inbox, write the need first: categorize English support messages into three labels, using local inference, within a stated hardware budget. This becomes the question you ask of each card. “Which model is best?” is too broad to produce a useful engineering decision. Record the publisher and exact model identifier. A family can contain base, instruction-tuned, quantized, and adapter releases. A revision identifies a particular state of the files; a moving branch name alone does not pin a reproducible artifact. A quantized release stores some values at reduced precision, a more compact way to represent each number. That can change resource use and behavior. Read the license file alongside the summary. Check the expected input format, supported task, runtime examples (instructions for the software that executes the model), limitations, and how reported evaluations were conducted. A benchmark score describes that benchmark's conditions; our own messages still require a separate check.

passages.title: Read a model card and check its license: Find evidence about a specific release
passages.text: Keep an evidence sheet with fields for release/revision, license, task, input format, runtime, hardware guidance, limitations, and verification performed. Mark an unknown as unknown. “Not tested here” is more useful than invented confidence. This lesson does not download or recommend a changing list of models. The build “Build a local model request tracer” shows the practice: it names its tested default model, records the test environment, and marks the alternatives it did not test.

passages.title: Read a model card and check its license: From requirements to a local test
passages.text: Start with the first box, the requirement: the task, input, output, privacy and hardware limits for the inbox. Use it to read the release evidence, which is the card, the files, the license and the runtime guidance. The local check then runs a candidate on your own representative messages. The order matters. The card helps you choose candidates, but only the local check shows whether a candidate meets your requirement.

Find one limitation and one item you cannot confirm. Do not download files or run code during this inspection. Check your understanding

passages.title: Read a model card and check its license: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Documentation can be incomplete or outdated. Descriptions of memory use depend on precision, context, runtime and workload. A release working in one runtime is not proof of compatibility with every runtime. Key takeaways - Write the requirement first. Then use the model card as evidence about one exact release and revision. - Keep three things apart in your notes: what the publisher documents, what you measured, and what is still unknown. - Before you report a result, record the revision you tested and the check you ran on your own messages. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - Hugging Face: model cards - Hugging Face: downloading a specific revision

passages.title: Read repeated-trial results, quality, latency, cost, and coverage: One run of a varying system is one sample
passages.text: The keyword rules in the earlier lessons gave the same output on every run. A model often does not. With sampling settings such as temperature, which Output limits, sampling, and streaming introduced, the same input can produce a different output on the next run. Then one pass on a case can be luck, and one fail can be bad luck. So an evaluation runs each case several times. Each attempt is a trial. For each case, count the trials that passed, failed and were incomplete, meaning they produced no output to grade. Three summaries answer different questions: - Share of trials passed. It fits work that makes a single attempt per message: it estimates how often one attempt succeeds. - Passed at least once in k trials. Some guides call this pass@k. It fits work where a person can retry and keep the first good result. - Passed in every one of k trials. Some guides call this pass^k. It fits work where the same kind of input keeps arriving and every occurrence must be handled correctly, such as account-security messages that must always be flagged.

passages.title: Read repeated-trial results, quality, latency, cost, and coverage: One run of a varying system is one sample
passages.text: “Passed in every trial” is much stricter than “passed at least once.” If each trial passes with probability 0.75 and the trials are independent, all three of three pass with probability 0.75 × 0.75 × 0.75, about 0.42. Quality is one column of the result A change can trade quality against other properties, so record them together: - Latency is the elapsed time for one trial, including any retry. Report it with the model, hardware and load that produced it. - Cost is what each trial consumes: model calls, tokens or money. - Coverage is the list of input kinds that the case set includes. A pass rate says nothing about a kind of input with no cases. What a report records Two results can be compared only when you know what produced each one. Record these beside every result:

passages.title: Read repeated-trial results, quality, latency, cost, and coverage: One run of a varying system is one sample
passages.text: - Case set and split: which version of the cases, and whether they were development or held-out cases. - System versions: the model, the prompt and any tools, each with its exact version or revision. - Grader versions: every grader, including a rubric's wording or a model-based grader's model and prompt. - Environment: the runtime, hardware and software versions, and any random seeds. - Trial count: how many trials each case received. - Results: passes, fails and incomplete trials for every case, beside latency, cost and coverage. The script below records its own version, Python version and seeds in its results file. The stand-in has no model, prompt or tools to version.

passages.title: Read repeated-trial results, quality, latency, cost, and coverage: Read five trials of six cases across three runs
passages.text: Each case enters the run and gets five trials. Each trial ends as pass, fail or incomplete. The per-case counts keep all three, plus the calls the trials used. The report then lists every case, not only an average, so a case that fails often stays visible. The data below comes from repeat_trials.py. The system is a stand-in: a small random program, not a model. For each case it returns the expected category with a fixed probability, a wrong category otherwise, and sometimes no output at all. The probabilities in stand_in.json were chosen for teaching and describe no real system. Fixed random seeds make the run reproducible. Configuration A makes one call per trial. Configuration B makes one more call when the first call produces no output. Each trial uses the same random draws in A and B, so B differs from A only where it retries. A second run of A uses different random draws, to show how much results vary between runs of the same configuration.

passages.title: Read repeated-trial results, quality, latency, cost, and coverage: Read five trials of six cases across three runs
passages.text: First compare A with B. B's verdicts match A's on every trial that A completed. They differ only on the trials where A produced no output. B retried each one: became passes, became fails and stayed incomplete. That cost extra calls. A retry turns a missing output into an output; it does not make that output correct. Then compare the two runs of A. Same configuration, same cases, different random draws: the totals moved from to passes, and refund-missing passed of 5 in the first run and of 5 in the second. That is variation between runs. With five trials, a difference of one or two passes on a case can come from variation alone, so it is not evidence that one configuration is better. Last, read the summaries. Every case passed at least once in every run, so “passed at least once” hides almost everything here. “Passed in every trial” separates the runs, but it moves between runs of the same configuration too.

passages.title: Read repeated-trial results, quality, latency, cost, and coverage: Read five trials of six cases across three runs
passages.text: The stand-in does no real work, so its timings mean nothing, and none are reported. In a real run, record the elapsed time of every trial. Each of B's retried trials includes the time of two calls, so a retry policy adds latency exactly where the first call produced no output. The model request tracer records real timings for one local model request, with its model and hardware. The six cases cover billing, delivery, account security, an out-of-scope question, ambiguous wording and a misleading word (“order” in a refund message). They leave out messages in other languages, messages with two problems, very long messages, and blank or missing input, which the rules must reject. Neither configuration has any result for those kinds of input.

passages.title: Read repeated-trial results, quality, latency, cost, and coverage: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Use the tables above. Your team must choose A or B for automatic triage: each message is triaged once, and nobody reviews the category. Write down which numbers support your choice, which numbers you would not trust yet, and two measurements you still need. Check your understanding

passages.title: Read repeated-trial results, quality, latency, cost, and coverage: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Real variation depends on the model, the prompt and the sampling settings, so record them with every run. Five trials per case are enough to read row by row and too few to rank two configurations. The 0.42 calculation assumes that trials are independent. Real failures often cluster on hard inputs, so measure every-trial consistency for each case directly instead of computing it from an average rate. Key takeaways - A system whose output varies needs several trials per case. One pass is one sample. - “Passed at least once” and “passed every time” answer different questions. Use the second when every occurrence of an input must succeed. - Record the case set and split, the model, prompt, tool and grader versions, the environment and the trial count beside every result, and report passes, fails and incomplete trials for every case with latency, cost and coverage. - A small gap between configurations can come from variation alone. Read the cases before trusting the totals. References Official references checked October 20, 2026.

passages.title: How models connect to retrieval, tools, and agents: The application supplies evidence and tools
passages.text: Retrieval, tools and agents do not change how a model generates text. Each changes what the application sends to the model or does with its output, and each change needs its own check. Our inbox assistant must answer a policy question, but its model weights may not contain the current policy. Retrieval means locating relevant information from a source. In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), the application searches approved policy documents and adds matching passages to the request. RAG changes the input, so check two things separately: did retrieval find the right passage, and does the answer agree with it? A tool is an operation the application exposes, such as looking up a shipment. A tool call is a request to execute that operation with supplied arguments. The model can only propose a call in its output. Application code must validate the arguments, authorize access, perform the action, and inspect the result. An agent is an application arrangement in which a model helps choose actions over multiple steps. A workflow makes those steps and transitions explicit. State is the information the workflow needs to continue, such as the current task and tool results. Every model request and tool call in that loop needs the checks above, and the workflow needs a defined way to stop.

passages.title: How models connect to retrieval, tools, and agents: The application supplies evidence and tools
passages.text: MCP standardizes interactions between applications and context/tool servers. A2A concerns interaction between agents. You do not need either protocol to understand our first model call. For the support example, start with the smallest workflow that meets the need: retrieve policy, draft answer, check evidence, request review. Add tools or agent-controlled branching only when the task requires them.

passages.title: How models connect to retrieval, tools, and agents: Retrieve evidence, draft and review
passages.text: Retrieve finds an approved policy passage and adds it to the request; this is the change to the model's input. Generate is the same kind of model request as in the earlier lessons, now with that passage as evidence. Validate and review compares the draft's claims with the passage and treats any proposed action, such as a refund, as a separate decision for application code. Notice that no box lets the model's text authorize an action on its own.

passages.title: How models connect to retrieval, tools, and agents: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Separate “tell me the refund policy” from “issue this refund.” For each request, list the information needed, the possible output, and whether an external action is required. Check your understanding

passages.title: How models connect to retrieval, tools, and agents: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Untrusted retrieved text can contain instructions. Supplying it as context must not grant tool permissions. More agents or more steps can increase cost and failure opportunities rather than improve a task. Key takeaways - Retrieval changes what the model receives; tools change what the application does with its output. - A tool call is a proposal. Application code validates, authorizes and executes it. Best practices - Before adding tools or agent steps, run the simpler retrieve, draft and review workflow on the same requests and compare results. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - MCP: architecture overview - A2A: key concepts

passages.title: State machines, branches, loops, and workflow graphs: Workflows turn “keep trying” into named steps and rules
passages.text: Our assistant drafts replies to support questions, and some drafts are wrong. One tempting fix is a prompt that says “check your answer and keep trying until it is right.” That sentence does not say which step runs next, what “right” means or when to give up. A workflow writes those rules down where code can follow them. The retrieval and tools lesson called state the information a workflow needs to continue. Here it becomes concrete data: for the support reply it holds the request, the chosen route, the current draft and an attempt counter. Each step reads the state and writes an update to it. A state machine is a fixed set of named states plus the transitions between them. Each transition happens only when its condition is true, and no other moves are possible. A simple traffic light is a state machine: green changes to yellow, yellow changes to red, and no other order is allowed.

passages.title: State machines, branches, loops, and workflow graphs: Workflows turn “keep trying” into named steps and rules
passages.text: A workflow graph draws the same idea as boxes and arrows. Nodes do the work and update the state. Edges decide which node runs next. A branch is a node with several outgoing edges and a rule that picks exactly one of them from the state. A loop is an edge that returns to an earlier node, so a step can run again. A loop must have an exit condition that code can check, such as “stop after three attempts.” Without one, a draft that never passes keeps the workflow running. LangGraph, a graph framework, shows the same pieces in its documentation: state, nodes, normal edges, conditional edges chosen by a routing function, and special start and end nodes. It also stops any run that exceeds a recursion limit, which defaults to 1,000 super-steps (rounds of node runs) from version 1.0.6, by raising GraphRecursionError. Treat that limit as a safety net. Your own attempt counter should end the loop long before it. The graph also explains the difference between a workflow and an agent. In a fixed workflow, code picks every edge. In an agent, the model picks among the edges the graph allows. Either way, the model cannot jump to “send the reply” if no edge leads there from the current node.

passages.title: State machines, branches, loops, and workflow graphs: Trace a draft through a branch and a loop
passages.text: Start at the first node, Classify the request. It writes a route into the state and is a branch: an action request, such as closing an account, takes the edge to Human review and ends there. A question takes the edge down to Draft a reply, which saves the draft in the state. Check the draft compares the draft with the policy and adds 1 to the attempt counter. It is a branch with three labelled outcomes. A pass leads to Send reply. A failure with tries left follows the cobalt edge back to drafting. A failure with no tries left leads to Escalate to a person. The check reads the counter from the state before it picks an edge. The loop ends because the state records how many times it has run, not because the model decides it has tried enough.

passages.title: State machines, branches, loops, and workflow graphs: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Use the support reply workflow graph from the previous step, with a limit of three attempts. For each request, write the nodes in the order they run and the final value of attempts. 1. A question whose first draft passes the check. 2. A question whose drafts fail every check. 3. A request to close the customer's account. Check your understanding

passages.title: State machines, branches, loops, and workflow graphs: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes A graph shows which moves are possible. It does not make each node correct: a weak check can still pass a wrong draft, and the graph will send it. Every pass through a loop is another model request, with its own cost and delay. Keep retry limits low and measure how often the loop runs. A branch rule that reads free-form model text, such as “the model said it looks fine,” is fragile. Prefer rules that read a field in the state, such as a check result or a counter. Key takeaways - State is the data the workflow carries. Nodes update it, and edges read it to choose the next node. - A branch picks one edge from the state. A loop returns to an earlier node and needs an exit condition that code can check. - In an agent, the model chooses among allowed edges; the graph still limits where it can go next. References Official references checked October 20, 2026. - LangGraph: Graph API overview (state, nodes, edges, recursion limit)

passages.title: Tasks, handoffs, retries, and durable state: Long work needs a record that outlives the process
passages.text: A refund request is not one quick step. The assistant looks up the order, asks the customer for a photo and may wait hours for it, sends the refund and then tells the customer. During that time the program can restart, or another agent or a person can take over. If the progress exists only in the program's memory, a restart either loses the work or repeats a step that should run once, such as the refund. A task is a unit of work with its own ID and a status that moves through a fixed lifecycle. The A2A specification, version 1.0, defines these task states: submitted, working, input-required, auth-required, completed, failed, canceled and rejected. Input-required and auth-required pause the task until the client, or an out-of-band step, supplies the input or credentials. The last four are terminal. A2A says a task in a terminal state does not restart; a follow-up request starts a new task in the same context. Durable state is progress saved outside the running process, for example in a database, so a new process can read it and continue. LangGraph calls its saved snapshots checkpoints and groups them by a thread_id. Its documentation warns that the in-memory checkpointer loses everything on restart and recommends a persistent one for production.

passages.title: Tasks, handoffs, retries, and durable state: Long work needs a record that outlives the process
passages.text: A handoff passes a task from one worker to another: an agent, a service or a person. The receiver needs the task record: the ID, the goal, the current state, the steps already done and what the task is waiting for. It does not need the sender's private memory. In A2A, the client tracks the remote agent's work by task ID and never sees the agent's internals. A retry runs a failed step again. A timeout is usually transient: the same call may work a few seconds later. A malformed order ID is permanent: repeating it fails every time. Temporal, a workflow engine, retries a failed activity by default with growing waits and no attempt limit, unless you set one. Its documentation says permanent failures are better surfaced than retried: list their error types as non-retryable in the Retry Policy, and mark errors non-retryable in activity code only sparingly.

passages.title: Tasks, handoffs, retries, and durable state: Long work needs a record that outlives the process
passages.text: Retries create one more risk. Temporal states that an activity may run more than once, and recommends making activities idempotent: running one twice has the same effect as running it once. Its suggested idempotency key combines the workflow run ID and the activity ID. The service being called enforces the key, not the worker: the payment service sees a key it already processed and returns the earlier result instead of paying again. The key must be the same on every attempt, including an attempt by a new process. Derive it from durable data, such as the task ID plus the step name, or write it into the task record before the first call. A key generated fresh on each attempt looks new to the service, so it does not protect a retry.

passages.title: Tasks, handoffs, retries, and durable state: Follow a task through its states
passages.text: A new task starts in Submitted and moves to Working, where it runs its next step. If a step fails with a transient error, the cobalt loop retries that step and the task stays in Working. When the task needs something from the user, it asks and moves to Input required. Nothing runs there; the task waits. The customer's reply moves it back to Working, which continues from the saved progress, not from the beginning. Working ends in one of three terminal states. Completed means the result is saved. Failed means no retry is left: the error is permanent, or the attempts ran out. Canceled means someone stopped the task. Every arrow changes the task record, so save the record before the task moves on. A crash then loses at most the step that was running.

passages.title: Tasks, handoffs, retries, and durable state: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: The refund worker crashes at three different moments. For each, decide what the new worker should do after it loads the task record. 1. After the record was saved with “lookup done,” before the refund step started. 2. After the payment service accepted the refund, but before the worker saved “refund done.” 3. While the task waits in Input required for the customer's photo. Check your understanding

passages.title: Tasks, handoffs, retries, and durable state: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes An idempotency key protects only services that check it. If a service ignores the key, a retry can still repeat its side effect, so confirm the behavior in that service's documentation. Unlimited retries can turn a permanent error into an endless loop of failing calls. Set an attempt limit and list the error types that cannot succeed as non-retryable. A handoff that sends the whole chat transcript instead of a task record makes the receiver guess the current state. It also passes along text that may contain instructions nobody should follow. Key takeaways - A task has an ID and a lifecycle. Paused states wait for input; terminal states end the task for good. - Durable state lets a new process or another worker continue from the saved record after a restart or a handoff. - Retry only steps that are safe to repeat. An idempotency key, enforced by the called service, keeps a retried side effect from happening twice. References Official references checked October 20, 2026, against A2A specification version 1.0. - A2A: life of a task - A2A specification: task states - LangGraph: persistence and checkpointers - Temporal: retry policies - Temporal: activity idempotency

passages.title: Write evaluation cases with inputs, expected outcomes, and failure criteria: Success criteria come before cases
passages.text: “Make the inbox better” cannot be graded. A grader needs a written statement of what a correct result is and what an unacceptable result is. Write that statement first, then write cases that test it. Our task has three parts. The inbox suggests one category from a fixed list: billing, delivery, account or other. It sets a review flag, needs_human, to true when a person must look at the message, such as a possible account takeover. And it rejects input that is not a message: blank text or a missing body raises ValueError, the same input contract as make_message in the programming exercises. The success criteria state what counts as correct for the whole task: one allowed category, the category a support lead would choose, the review flag whenever account security is at risk, and a rejection for input that is not a message. Each case then makes those criteria concrete for one input. A useful case has four parts:

passages.title: Write evaluation cases with inputs, expected outcomes, and failure criteria: Success criteria come before cases
passages.text: - The input: the exact message the system receives. - The expected outcome: the category a correct system returns, or the rejection it must raise. - The failure criteria: conditions that fail the case even when the expected outcome is met. Write them as data the grader checks. For the password case, the failure criterion is needs_human set to false: a correct account category still fails, because a possible takeover would wait in an ordinary queue. Most cases have none; an extra review flag on a billing message costs a person's time but harms nobody. - The class: the kind of input the case represents, so you can see which kinds the set covers. Each case also carries a short why: the written reason for its expectation. The grader does not read it. A reviewer reads it when a verdict looks wrong. Choose cases that can fail in different ways

passages.title: Write evaluation cases with inputs, expected outcomes, and failure criteria: Success criteria come before cases
passages.text: Eight cases cannot represent real traffic, but each one can test a different risk. Two are typical messages. One, the password case, tests the review flag. Two test where a behavior should not happen: a laptop question must not enter a support queue, and the word “order” in a refund message must not pull it into delivery. A case set that only checks where a behavior should happen rewards a system that does it everywhere. Three cases are edge cases. A blank message and a message with no body must both be rejected. An ambiguous message, “I was charged after I closed my account,” needs a decision written into the case: an unexpected charge is billing, even when the account is mentioned. Without a written decision, two reviewers can grade the same output differently.

passages.title: Write evaluation cases with inputs, expected outcomes, and failure criteria: Grade each case against its criteria
passages.text: The grader runs the case and takes the first exit that applies. If the system produced no output, because it crashed or returned nothing, the case is incomplete. If the system raised the rejection the case expects, the case passes: rejecting blank text is the required behavior. Otherwise the output goes through four checks in order. If the case expects a rejection, any output fails: the system returned a category where it had to refuse. The contract check fails an unknown label or a missing flag. The outcome check fails a category that differs from the expected one. The failure criterion check fails an output that meets any listed condition. An output that clears every check passes. The rules here give the same output on every run, so each case has one trial. The table shows the actual verdicts. A short Python script, grade_cases.py, ran a few keyword rules on the eight cases above. The rules are not a model, so every run gives the same verdicts.

passages.title: Write evaluation cases with inputs, expected outcomes, and failure criteria: Grade each case against its criteria
passages.text: Notice the three results that differ from an ordinary pass. password-changed has the correct category and still fails on its failure criterion. blank-message passes because the rules raised the expected ValueError. missing-body is incomplete: the rules tried to read text from a missing body and crashed with AttributeError, so no output reached the grader. That crash is a bug in the rules, not a wrong answer. The summary is passed, failed and incomplete, out of . Counting the crash as a fail would hide it among wrong answers. Dropping it would hide that one input produced nothing.

passages.title: Write evaluation cases with inputs, expected outcomes, and failure criteria: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Write one new case on paper for this message: “Please change the email address on my account.” Give the input, the expected outcome, any failure criteria, a class and a why. Then rewrite the vague criterion “the reply should be helpful” as two statements that a grader could check. Check your understanding

passages.title: Write evaluation cases with inputs, expected outcomes, and failure criteria: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes An expected outcome encodes a judgment, and that judgment can be wrong. When a verdict looks unfair, read the case's why before you change the system. Failure criteria catch only the conditions someone listed: a reply that is harmful in a way nobody wrote down still passes. Key takeaways - Write the success criteria for the task first. Each case then makes them concrete for one input. - A case has an input, an expected outcome, failure criteria and a class. Write failure criteria as conditions the grader can check. - A required rejection is an expected outcome, so it passes. A crash with no output is incomplete. - Include cases where a behavior must not happen, and write decisions into ambiguous cases. References Official references checked October 20, 2026. - Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents — a task as defined inputs and success criteria; testing where a behavior should and should not occur. - OpenAI: Evaluation best practices — defining success criteria first; including typical, edge and adversarial cases.

passages.title: Run a Python file and read its output: The shell launches the Python interpreter
passages.text: Every later build on aiml starts the same way: you type a command, a Python program runs, and you read what it prints. When something goes wrong, you need to know which of those three parts failed. This lesson names the parts and runs one small program. A program is a set of instructions a computer executes. Python is the language used for many examples on aiml. Its interpreter reads and executes Python instructions. You will use ordinary text files to keep those instructions. A terminal lets you type commands to programs. The shell interprets those commands. The folder you are currently working in is your working directory. A command such as python3 inbox.py asks the Python interpreter to run a file in that directory; it is not Python source to paste inside the file. Install a supported Python version using the instructions for your operating system on the official Python website. The downloadable exercises here use Python 3.11 or later. Open a terminal and run python3 --version. On some Windows installations, the command is py instead; use the equivalent command throughout.

passages.title: Run a Python file and read its output: The shell launches the Python interpreter
passages.text: Create a folder called aiml-foundations. Download and extract the exercise archive into it, then open a terminal in the directory containing inbox.py. A path describes where a file is located. If Python reports that it cannot open the file, compare the current folder with the file's location before changing code. Run python3 inbox.py. The file creates a small message object and prints JSON. You will learn those terms in the next lessons. The program only handles data; it does not run or train an AI model.

passages.title: Run a Python file and read its output: From a Python file to terminal output
passages.text: The flow starts with the source file, inbox.py, which holds Python instructions. The command python3 inbox.py tells the interpreter which file to execute. What leaves is terminal output: the printed result or a reported error. Read which stage reported an error: if Python cannot open the file, the interpreter never executed any of your instructions, so the problem is the path, not the code.

passages.title: Run a Python file and read its output: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Download the foundation exercise archive, extract it, and open its foundations folder. Run: The second command should print: Open inbox.py in a text editor. Change only the question inside its final make_message call, save it, and run the command again. Predict which output field will change. Check your understanding

passages.title: Run a Python file and read its output: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Commands differ across operating systems and installations. The examples do not install Python for you. No paid account, model download, or third-party Python package is required for these exercises. Key takeaways - The shell runs your command; the interpreter executes the instructions in the Python file. - Read the exact command, file path, and error before debugging behavior. Best practices - Use a dedicated exercise folder and keep the original archive. - Change one thing at a time and compare the actual output. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - Python: setup and usage - Python: first language examples

passages.title: Write tests and inspect failures: Tests compare behavior with a contract
passages.text: In the previous lessons you ran make_message, read_message and the HTTP fixture by hand and compared the output yourself. A test does that comparison for you, so you can repeat it after every change and see at once what broke. A test case supplies conditions and checks expected behavior. An assertion states what must be true. A test suite collects cases that can be run together. The supplied exercises use Python's standard-library unittest module. A unit test checks a small behavior in isolation, such as rejecting blank message content. An integration test checks connected parts, such as an HTTP client talking to our fixture server. A fixture is controlled test input or supporting state. Our HTTP fixture is deterministic: it returns the same known JSON object every time. Read the invalid-input cases. Passing whitespace or a number must raise an explicit error. A valid user-message object must survive a JSON round trip. A list, an assistant-role object, and malformed JSON must be rejected at the expected boundaries. A useful failure is reproducible and tells us which expectation broke. A regression is a previously correct behavior that fails after a change. Keeping small cases lets us detect changes without manually inspecting every response.

passages.title: Write tests and inspect failures: Tests compare behavior with a contract
passages.text: Later model evaluation uses labelled tasks, source checks and workload measurements. The vocabulary overlaps, but a passing Python test suite cannot stand in for those independent checks.

passages.title: Write tests and inspect failures: Trace a test from input to assertion
passages.text: A test starts from a fixture: a known input such as ' ' or '{broken'. It runs the real implementation, make_message, read_message or exchange, not a copy of it. An assertion then compares what happened with the contract, for example that ' ' raises ValueError. Notice that a rejected input can be a passing test: the contract says that input must fail.

passages.title: Write tests and inspect failures: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Run the suite from the exercise folder: It contains seven test methods across message validation and the local HTTP fixture. Read the message tests: In a copy of the source, remove the blank-input rejection and run the suite again. Predict which assertion fails. Restore the check and confirm the suite passes. Check your understanding

passages.title: Write tests and inspect failures: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Tests cover only their asserted behavior. A fixture response can hide real provider differences, so later Build articles separately identify live integration checks and output-quality evaluation. Key takeaways - Test the contract, including expected rejection and failures. - Unit tests, integration tests and model evaluations provide different evidence. - A test is useful when it fails after a meaningful behavior change, as the invalid-input test does in the activity. Best practices - Keep fixtures small and meaningful. - Describe exactly what passed and what remains untested. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - Python: unittest

passages.title: What are tokens and tokenizers?: How text becomes vocabulary IDs
passages.text: You send a model the sentence “AI models learn patterns.” Before the model can process it, a tokenizer converts that text into integers. Which integers it produces depends on the tokenizer's vocabulary and splitting rules. A token is one of those text units. It can contain a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or spaces. Its token ID is the integer that identifies its entry in the vocabulary. The vocabulary is the tokenizer's collection of supported entries and their IDs. For this lesson, we ran OpenAI's o200k_base encoding with tiktoken 0.14.0. It encodes that exact sentence as : five tokens for four words. The diagram in the next step shows the text associated with each ID. You can inspect the recorded output and the script that produced it. An ID is a lookup key, not a score or a measure of meaning. ID 17527 does not mean “more intelligent” or “more important” than ID 13. In a neural language model, an embedding is a learned list of numbers associated with an input ID. Looking up that list is a later model operation; tokenizing the sentence does not train or run the model.

passages.title: What are tokens and tokenizers?: How text becomes vocabulary IDs
passages.text: The word embedding has a second meaning on this site. In “What jobs do different models do?”, an embedding model returns one vector for a whole input text so that texts can be compared. In this lesson, an embedding is the learned list a language model looks up for each token ID. Tokenization matters when an application needs to stay within an input allowance. Counting four words would undercount this five-token example. The next examples also show why even an unchanged token count can hide a different input sequence.

passages.title: What are tokens and tokenizers?: Inspect a recorded tokenization
passages.text: Read the diagram from text to IDs: 1. The tokenizer receives the exact string, including spaces and the final period. 2. The selected encoding splits it into pieces. A space is part of each of the pieces models, learn, and patterns; the period is a separate piece. 3. Each piece has an ID in this vocabulary. The output is an ordered sequence, not an unordered collection of words. 4. The model can use the IDs to look up its learned embeddings and process the sequence. Changing the period to ! keeps the count at five but changes the final ID from 13 to 0 in this encoding. Counting tokens alone would miss that input change. The explorer lets you compare the two recorded sequences directly.

passages.title: What are tokens and tokenizers?: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Use the selector below for three comparisons. Each option displays a recording from the same tokenizer: - Compare the AI statement with its punctuation variant. Find the piece and ID that changed. - Compare “Hello” with “ Hello”. Both have one token. Check whether their IDs are the same. - Select the accented word. Inspect the pieces and their bytes to see how the encoding represents it. The text is shown in quotes so a leading space is visible. Selecting a token shows its actual ID and UTF-8 bytes from the recording. These are fixed examples you can inspect without installing Python. Check your understanding Reproduce the recording in Python If you want to run the encoder, download record.py and fixture.json into one directory. Create a virtual environment there and install the pinned tokenizer package: The first online run can download the vocabulary file from OpenAI. The script checks that its generated examples match the supplied JSON file, a text format for structured data. Its success message is Verified 6 raw-text examples with o200k_base. It also supports --offline --cache-dir PATH when that directory already contains the verified vocabulary file.

passages.title: What are tokens and tokenizers?: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes The five-token result describes this raw string and this encoding. A chat request can add role markers, separators and other formatting before tokenization. Count the input as the selected model or service actually formats it; do not use a word count or a different tokenizer as an exact substitute. Hugging Face's chat-template guide shows how messages become a formatted token sequence. The visible pieces in this lesson all decode as UTF-8 text individually. That is not guaranteed for every token: some byte-level tokens represent only part of a multi-byte character. Keep the bytes or decode the complete sequence when inspecting unfamiliar text. The token ID alone does not tell you a token's text, meaning or model behavior. Key takeaways - A named tokenizer and exact input produce a sequence of vocabulary IDs. - Words, tokens and embeddings describe different things. - Spaces and punctuation can change IDs even when the token count stays the same. Best practices - Record the encoding name and tokenizer version with an example's IDs and counts. - Preserve exact input text when investigating a count or reproducing a failure. References Sources and local recording checked October 18, 2026:

passages.title: What are tokens and tokenizers?: Limits, takeaways and references
