passages.title: Tool schemas, execution, and permissions: What a tool definition promises, and what it cannot
passages.text: Our support assistant now has two tools. lookup_order reads the status of an order. issue_refund sends money back to a customer. A customer writes, “My order arrived broken. Refund it.” The model answers with a request to call issue_refund. Something must decide whether money actually moves. This lesson shows what that something is. A tool definition is the description the application gives the model for one tool. It has a name, a plain-language description and an input schema. A schema is a machine-readable rule for which arguments a call may contain. MCP tool definitions write it in JSON Schema. Read it one field at a time. required lists the arguments every call must include. enum limits reason to three values. additionalProperties: false rejects any argument the schema does not name. Without that line, JSON Schema accepts extra keys. Notice what is missing: the customer. The application already knows who is signed in from its own session. If the schema accepted a customer_id, any text that persuaded the model could name a different customer. Identity and authority come from application state, not from arguments the model writes.

passages.title: Tool schemas, execution, and permissions: What a tool definition promises, and what it cannot
passages.text: The retrieval and tools lesson said that application code validates, authorizes and executes a proposed call. This lesson separates those three steps. Tool execution means the application performs the operation that the call names. Permission, also called authorization, is the decision whether this caller may perform this action on this object now. The schema answers “is the call well formed?” Permission answers “is the call allowed?” A call can pass the first check and fail the second, for example a valid order ID that belongs to someone else. Tools also differ in their effects. lookup_order only reads. issue_refund has a side effect: it changes something outside the conversation, and deleting a chat message does not undo it. Applications usually apply stricter rules to side-effect tools. The MCP specification asks for human control over every tool, not only these: there SHOULD always be a human who can deny any tool invocation, and clients MUST treat tool annotations, a server's hints about how a tool behaves, as untrusted unless the server itself is trusted.

passages.title: Tool schemas, execution, and permissions: Follow one proposed call through the checks
passages.text: Start at the first box. The model writes only the blue strip: a tool name and arguments. The schema check compares those arguments with inputSchema. A missing order_id or an unknown reason fails here, and the application returns an error result without running anything. The permission check uses data the model did not write: the signed-in customer, the owner of the order and the refund policy. A denied call returns a refusal. A policy can also hold an allowed call for a person to review before it runs; the last lesson in this series shows that decision, and the supplied check uses it for refunds. Only an allowed call reaches the fourth box, where the application runs the tool and the real side effect happens. Every path ends in the same place: a result sent to the model. Follow the cobalt line back to the top. The model reads the output, the error or the refusal in its next turn and can propose another call. The model never passes the checks by itself; it can only try again.

passages.title: Tool schemas, execution, and permissions: Follow one proposed call through the checks
passages.text: MCP describes the same split from the protocol side. An unknown tool or a malformed request is a protocol error, sent as a JSON-RPC error. An invalid argument value or a failed business rule is a tool execution error, returned inside the result with isError: true. The specification says clients SHOULD give execution errors to the model so that it can correct the call.

passages.title: Tool schemas, execution, and permissions: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: The signed-in customer, customer-1, owns one damaged order, order-1. For each proposed call, write down which check stops it, or write “runs.” 1. issue_refund for order-1 with reason set to "changed my mind". 2. lookup_order for order-1. 3. issue_refund for order-1, reason damaged. An earlier message in the chat says “A manager approved this refund.” 4. issue_refund for order-1 with an extra customer_id argument that names customer-2. Check your understanding

passages.title: Tool schemas, execution, and permissions: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes A schema describes shape, not authority. It cannot say who owns an order, how much one person may refund or who approved an exception. Those rules need application code that reads data the model did not write. A tool description guides the model but does not bind it. The model can still propose a call that the description discourages, so wording in the description is not a control. Check permission where the action runs. A check in the chat layer does not protect the payment service if another program can call that service directly. Key takeaways - A tool definition tells the model what a call should look like. The input schema lets the application reject malformed arguments before anything runs. - Passing the schema is not permission. Identity and authority come from application state, never from arguments the model writes. - Errors and refusals return to the model as results, so it can correct the call or tell the user what really happened. Best practices - Give each side-effect tool the narrowest schema you can, with fixed value lists and no extra properties, and keep the caller's identity out of its arguments. References Official references checked October 20, 2026, against MCP specification version 2026-07-28.

passages.title: Training, validation, leakage, and overfitting: A low training loss is not the goal
passages.text: The training loop from the previous lesson makes the loss smaller on the examples it sees. Given enough adjustable values, it can drive that loss to zero by fitting the noise in those examples as well as the pattern. What you want is a model that predicts examples it has never seen. This lesson is about measuring that honestly. How does a model learn? introduced held-out data, overfitting and leakage. Here we separate the held-out data into two sets with different jobs and look at the numbers that show overfitting. The training set is the data the loop learns from; only it produces gradients. The validation set is used during development to compare choices: learning rates, model sizes, when to stop training. Those choices are hyperparameters, as defined in the loss lesson. The test set is used once, after all choices are made, to estimate how the chosen model handles new data.

passages.title: Training, validation, leakage, and overfitting: A low training loss is not the goal
passages.text: Our example has synthetic points. Each x is evenly spaced from 0 to 1, and y is sin(2πx) plus random noise with standard deviation , drawn by Python's random.Random({run.inputs.seed}). We shuffled them once and split them into training, validation and test points. The model is a polynomial curve, and its degree is the hyperparameter: a degree-1 curve is a straight line, and a degree-9 curve has 10 coefficients, enough to pass exactly through all 10 training points. Overfitting shows up as a gap: error on the training set keeps falling while error on the validation set stops falling and rises. Underfitting is the opposite problem: both errors stay high because the model cannot represent the pattern. Leakage is information that would not be available at prediction time reaching the model during development. It makes evaluation scores look better than real use will be. Four common forms:

passages.title: Training, validation, leakage, and overfitting: A low training loss is not the goal
passages.text: - Duplicates: the same or nearly the same example in training and evaluation sets. - Preprocessing on all data: computing averages, vocabularies or feature selections from the whole dataset before splitting. - Groups and time: messages from one customer, or from a later week, split across both sides when real use would only have the past. - Reusing the test set: checking the test score after each change, which turns the test set into a second validation set.

passages.title: Training, validation, leakage, and overfitting: Each split has one job
passages.text: The first figure shows the jobs as a process. All examples are split once. The training set feeds the box that fits weights. The fitted model goes to the comparison box, which scores it on the validation set. The return path, labeled change settings, goes back to fitting as many times as development needs. Only the chosen model goes on to the test set, and no path returns from the test result into any choice. The second figure lists the three sets side by side, because they are separate collections with separate roles, not stages of one process.

passages.title: Training, validation, leakage, and overfitting: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: The script splits.py fitted each degree on the training points and measured mean squared error (MSE) on the training and validation points; splits.json holds its output and the points below. Read the table. Which degree would you choose, and what do you expect its test error to be compared with its validation error? Check your understanding

passages.title: Training, validation, leakage, and overfitting: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes A clean split only protects you from the data you have. If the test set does not look like the messages the model will meet in use, a good test score still says little about that use. Removing exact duplicates misses near-duplicates, such as a message quoted in a reply. Every validation check spends a little of the set's value, so after many comparisons even validation scores become optimistic, and a fresh set is needed. Key takeaways - Training data fits weights, validation data chooses settings, and test data estimates the final result once. - Overfitting shows as training error falling while validation error rises. Watch both numbers, not only the training loss. - Split first, then fit any preprocessing on the training set only. Check for duplicates, shared customers and future data across splits before you trust a score. References Official references checked October 20, 2026. - Google Machine Learning Crash Course: dividing the original dataset - Google Machine Learning Crash Course: interpreting loss curves - scikit-learn 1.9: common pitfalls and data leakage

passages.title: Embeddings, vectors, similarity, and index compatibility: Compare meanings instead of shared words
passages.text: BM25 could not help with the query shrink a model for a laptop. The quantization note, “Quantization stores model weights with fewer bits to reduce memory,” answers that need, but it shares only the word model with the query. We need a comparison that can treat “shrink” and “fewer bits” as related ideas. A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as [0.9, 0.1, 0.2]. Each position is a coordinate, and the number of positions is the vector's dimension. This example has dimension 3. An embedding model is a model that reads a text and outputs a vector, called an embedding. It is trained so that texts with related meanings get vectors that point in similar directions. For example, the model sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on Hugging Face outputs vectors with 384 coordinates. Its model card lists the Apache-2.0 license. A real embedding has hundreds of coordinates, and no single coordinate has a name you can read. To make the arithmetic visible, this lesson uses hand-made teaching vectors with three named coordinates: . We wrote these numbers ourselves. No embedding model produced them; treat them as the output of an imaginary model A.

passages.title: Embeddings, vectors, similarity, and index compatibility: Compare meanings instead of shared words
passages.text: Cosine similarity compares the directions of two vectors. Multiply the matching coordinates and add the products; this sum is the dot product. Then divide by the length of each vector. The length is the square root of the sum of the squared coordinates. The result is 1 when two vectors point the same way, 0 when they share no direction and −1 when they point in opposite directions. For vectors scaled to length 1, the dot product already equals the cosine.

passages.title: Embeddings, vectors, similarity, and index compatibility: Embed the query, compare it with stored vectors, rank
passages.text: The flow starts at index time. The embedding model turns each note into a vector, and the index stores those vectors before any query arrives. At query time, the same model turns the query into a vector. The search system computes the cosine similarity between the query vector and every stored vector, then sorts the notes by that number. The table holds the stored vectors from the first box and the query vector from the second box. In every vector, coordinate 1 is “,” coordinate 2 is “” and coordinate 3 is “.” Text Vector Cosine with query Query: shrink a model for a laptop n1 quantization n2 tokenizer n3 training n4 inference n5 context window n6 memory planning ? Follow the third box for n1. The products of matching coordinates are , so the dot product is . The query vector has length and the n1 vector has length . The cosine is ÷ ( × ) = . The tokenizer note n2 points in a different direction, so its cosine is . The full ranking is . The quantization note now ranks first, although it shares only one word with the query. The comparison works only because the query and the notes were embedded by the same model: coordinate 1 means the same thing in every vector.

passages.text: Compute the cosine similarity between the query vector and the n6 vector . Write the three products, the dot product, both lengths and the cosine. Keep full precision until the end, and round only the final cosine to three decimal places. To reproduce the numbers, download similarity_trace.py and run it with Python 3.10 or newer. It also records the two index mismatches described in the next step. Compare its output with the recorded trace. Check your understanding

passages.title: Embeddings, vectors, similarity, and index compatibility: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes A vector index fixes its dimension when you create it. The FAISS library, for example, builds an index for vectors of one dimension d, and every added or queried vector must have d coordinates. The script checks the length the same way: when it compares a four-coordinate query with the three-coordinate index, it stops with this error: . That failure is easy to notice. The silent failure is worse. Suppose a different embedding model B also outputs three coordinates, but its coordinates mean other things. The script sends the same query through model B, which gives , and compares it with the model A index. No error appears, and the ranking becomes : the tokenizer note now ranks first. Record the model name and version with the index, and embed the whole collection again when you change the model. An embedding model reads a limited amount of text. The all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model card says it truncates input longer than 256 word pieces, so the end of a long document does not affect its vector. Split long documents into passages before you embed them.

passages.title: Embeddings, vectors, similarity, and index compatibility: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: For a large collection, comparing the query with every stored vector becomes slow. Approximate nearest-neighbor indexes search a smaller part of the collection. They are faster, but they can miss some of the closest vectors. Key takeaways - An embedding is a vector that an embedding model outputs for a text. Related meanings get vectors with similar directions. - Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by both vector lengths. It ranks direction, not correctness. - Query vectors and stored vectors must come from the same model. A matching dimension does not prove that. References Official references checked October 20, 2026. - Sentence Transformers: semantic search - Hugging Face model card: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 - FAISS wiki: getting started

passages.title: Weights, layers, activations, and neural networks: A network is layers of weighted sums
passages.text: The previous lesson multiplied a batch by a weight matrix and added a bias. That operation is a layer, the building block of a neural network. This lesson looks inside it: what one weight does, why a network stacks several layers, and what has to sit between them. A unit (often called a neuron) takes several input numbers. It multiplies each input by its own weight, adds the products, and adds one more learned number, the bias. The result is a weighted sum. A large positive weight makes its input push the sum up; a negative weight pushes it down; a weight near zero makes the unit ignore that input. A linear layer (also called a fully connected or dense layer) is a set of units that all read the same inputs, each with its own weights. A layer with 3 inputs and 4 units has a (3, 4) weight matrix and 4 biases. PyTorch's nn.Linear computes exactly this, for every row of a batch. An activation function is applied to each weighted sum after the layer. The common choice ReLU returns the sum when it is positive and 0 otherwise. The output of a unit after its activation is called its activation.

passages.title: Weights, layers, activations, and neural networks: A network is layers of weighted sums
passages.text: A neural network connects layers so that each layer's activations become the next layer's inputs. Layers between the input and the final output are hidden layers. The weights and biases of all layers are the network's parameters, the values that training changes. Everything else in the computation is fixed by the design of the network, called its architecture. Our example network has 3 inputs, one hidden layer of 4 units with ReLU, and an output layer of 2 units, one score per category. It has 3 × 4 + 4 + 4 × 2 + 2 = parameters.

passages.title: Weights, layers, activations, and neural networks: Trace one input through two layers
passages.text: The first figure zooms in on one unit. The three boxes labeled input 1 to input 3 each feed their own weight box, labeled × w1 to × w3. The products and the box labeled + bias meet in the weighted-sum box, and the ReLU box turns that sum into the unit's output. For our input and the first hidden unit, the weights are , so the products are . The bias is and the sum is . ReLU keeps because it is positive. The second figure runs the whole network on the same input. The hidden layer produces four weighted sums. The third sum is negative, so ReLU replaces it with 0, and that unit contributes nothing to the output for this input. The output layer then combines the four activations into two scores. The table lists every input and every intermediate value. Rows of W1 belong to the three inputs, and its columns to the four hidden units. Running the input through the network once, from first layer to last, is a forward pass. It is the "predict" part of training and the whole of inference.

passages.title: Weights, layers, activations, and neural networks: Trace one input through two layers
passages.text: Now remove ReLU and run the same two layers again: the output is . A single layer with weights W1·W2 = and bias b1·W2 + b2 = gives exactly the same . Without an activation, two linear layers collapse into one linear layer, so adding layers adds parameters but no new kinds of patterns. The bend that ReLU puts at zero is what lets stacked layers represent more than one layer can. The script network.py produces every value in this lesson; its saved output is network.json.

passages.title: Weights, layers, activations, and neural networks: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Do not read a single weight as an explanation of a prediction. A unit's effect depends on its inputs, on the other weights and on which later units are active. In real networks that interaction runs across millions or billions of parameters. Our hand-picked weights were chosen to make the arithmetic readable; trained weights start from small random values and are not designed by anyone. Units that ReLU keeps at 0 for every input stop learning, a failure often called a dead unit. Key takeaways - A unit computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, then applies an activation function. - A layer's weights have shape (inputs, units). Parameters are all the weights and biases; training changes only them. - Without an activation between them, stacked linear layers are equivalent to one linear layer. References Official references checked October 20, 2026. - PyTorch 2.14: torch.nn.Linear - PyTorch 2.14: torch.nn.ReLU - PyTorch: build the neural network tutorial

passages.title: What is a model?: A model combines structure and learned weights
passages.text: A model is a learned mapping from inputs to outputs. For our inbox, the input is a support message and the output might be scores for billing, delivery, and account issues. The application can turn those scores into a suggested label. A model is not the whole website. It does not automatically contain the website's customer database, sign-in system, or refund policy. Those are separate components the application must connect deliberately. Many models contain parameters: adjustable numerical values. The learned parameter values are often called weights. Architecture describes how the computation is arranged. To run a neural model, a runtime, the software that executes compatible model computations, combines an architecture with compatible weights. The input must also be prepared in the format the model expects. Think about two inbox models with the same arrangement of operations but weights learned from different examples. They can give different predictions for the same message. Sharing an architecture name does not mean they have identical behavior. A saved set of model values is often called a checkpoint. A release can also include configuration and files that prepare inputs. Saving a checkpoint makes it possible to load learned values later; it does not mean the saved model will understand every task.

passages.title: What is a model?: A model combines structure and learned weights
passages.text: For now, you do not need to calculate the model's scores. Follow the boundary: input enters a particular learned model, output leaves it, and the application decides what to do next.

passages.title: What is a model?: From a support message to category scores
passages.text: Follow the three boxes in order. A support message such as “I was charged twice.” is prepared and passed to the model. The architecture and learned weights turn it into a score for each category: billing, delivery and account. Only the scores leave the model. The customer database, the sign-in system and the decision about what to do with the scores are not inside the middle box. The application must handle them.

passages.title: What is a model?: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: A support inbox has four parts: the customer database, a checkpoint file, the runtime, and the application code. On paper or in a text editor, write which part does each of these jobs: 1. Loads the learned values and computes category scores for a message. 2. Decides whether to show a suggestion, send it to a reviewer or refuse an action. 3. Stores customer addresses and order history. 4. Holds the learned weights while nothing is running. Then answer one more question: if the model needs a customer's order number, which part must send it? Check your understanding

passages.title: What is a model?: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Model size is commonly reported as a parameter count. More parameters alone do not make a model better for your particular task. Learned values can encode unwanted patterns as well as useful ones. Key takeaways - Weights are the learned values; the architecture arranges the computation that uses them. - Model, weights, runtime, and application name different parts of a system. The model receives only the data the application passes to it. - A checkpoint records learned state, not quality. Record which exact model artifact produced a result. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - PyTorch: save and load a model - Hugging Face: model configuration

passages.title: How AI works: from input to prediction: AI, ML and deep learning
passages.text: A customer sends a support message: “I was charged twice.” We want the inbox to suggest the category billing, so the right person can review it. The task is called classification: assigning an input to a category. A chatbot, a large model and a complicated framework are not prerequisites for describing that task. Three terms help us place it: Artificial intelligence (AI)A broad field concerned with systems that perform tasks such as understanding language, recognizing patterns and solving problems. Machine learning (ML)An approach within AI where a model learns behavior from data. In our inbox, previously categorized messages can become training examples. Deep learningA form of machine learning using neural networks with multiple layers. A neural network is a computation with adjustable values learned during training. These are related ideas: deep learning sits within machine learning, and machine learning sits within AI. AI also includes approaches beyond learning from data. Our keyword rule in the next step is a simple software baseline; adding an if statement does not, by itself, make an application an AI system. For this series, keep asking two questions: Which part learns from examples? What does the surrounding application still have to do?

passages.title: How AI works: from input to prediction: Rules and learned models
passages.text: There are different ways to suggest a category for the same message. The important distinction is how the behavior was defined. A written rule“charged” → billingA developer writes the condition. Whenever the message contains that word, this rule suggests billing.Changing the behavior means changing the rule. A learned modelexamples → learned patternsTraining uses messages with their categories to adjust a model. The model then predicts a category for another message.Improving it can involve better examples, training or a different model. The rule is easy to inspect. It also misses “I paid twice”, which does not contain “charged.” It can misroute “I wasn’t charged; I can’t sign in” because that sentence does contain the keyword. A learned model may recognize different ways to describe the same problem. That depends on what it learned and how it is tested. It can still make the wrong prediction. Learned behavior does not mean every output must be random. A model can produce a repeatable result. The distinction here is that its behavior was fitted using data rather than expressed entirely as a list of hand-written conditions. These are teaching examples. We have not trained or measured a classifier in this lesson.

passages.title: How AI works: from input to prediction: Follow one prediction
passages.text: Now put a learned classifier inside the inbox. It is one part of a larger application. The application receives the message and passes the relevant text to a model. The model suggests a category. The application displays that suggestion and decides what happens next. Receiving a message, storing it, checking who is signed in and recording a review are ordinary software responsibilities. A model prediction does not replace those responsibilities. In particular, “billing” is a prediction, not authorization to refund money. A refund needs a separate application policy and permission check. The same distinction applies when an AI system proposes a database change, sends an email or calls a tool.

passages.title: How AI works: from input to prediction: Try it yourself
passages.text: Write these five jobs on paper: 1. Receive a support message. 2. Suggest its category. 3. Display the suggestion to a reviewer. 4. Store the reviewer's decision. 5. Issue a refund. For each job, ask: does it need learned behavior, ordinary application code, or an explicit permission check? More than one can apply.

passages.title: How AI works: from input to prediction: Where this can fail
passages.text: A useful-looking example is only a starting point. Check the boundaries of the actual task: - Ambiguous messages. A customer can mention billing while asking about a different problem. - Unfamiliar inputs. A model trained on one set of messages may perform poorly on a different language, product or customer group. - The wrong success check. Returning a category proves that the program returned something. It does not prove the category is useful or correct. - An unsafe connection to actions. A mistaken category becomes more serious if it automatically triggers a privileged operation. Start with a clear input, an expected kind of output and a review path for mistakes.

passages.title: How AI works: from input to prediction: Check your understanding
passages.text: Before opening the explanation, answer these questions: 1. If a classifier uses a neural network with several layers, can it be described as AI, ML and deep learning? 2. Does receiving a support message require a learned model? 3. Why does the keyword rule “charged” → billing miss “I paid twice”?

passages.title: How AI works: from input to prediction: Key takeaways
passages.text: - AI is a broad field. Machine learning and deep learning describe related approaches within it. - A written rule gets its behavior from a developer's conditions. A learned model gets part of its behavior from training data. - A working AI application includes software around its model: input handling, storage, review and permissions. - A prediction is a suggestion to the application. It does not grant permission to act.

passages.title: How AI works: from input to prediction: Engineering best practices
passages.text: Use these habits before choosing a model or a framework: - Name the task. “Suggest a support category” is concrete enough to test. - Define the output. Decide which categories are allowed and how someone reviews a wrong suggestion. - Keep a simple baseline. A small rule helps reveal what a learned model would need to improve. - Test beyond the demonstration. Include different wording and ambiguous messages before claiming that the system works reliably. The next lesson looks inside the word model: what is saved, what is learned and how an input becomes an output.

passages.title: What is an evaluation, and how does it differ from a unit test?: A unit test checks code; an evaluation checks a task
passages.text: In Checking correctness, latency, and failures, one inbox reply finished, had a valid category, and still had the wrong category. That was one message. Suppose you change the prompt and want to know whether the inbox now does better. You need the same comparison on many messages, made the same way each time, and written down. That repeated, recorded comparison is an evaluation. A unit test and an evaluation both compare what happened with what should happen. They answer different questions. A unit test checks that one piece of code follows its contract. In the foundation exercises, make_message(" ") must raise ValueError. The code always behaves the same way for the same input, so the test must pass on every run. One failure means a bug. An evaluation runs a system on a set of cases and records how each output compares with that case's success criteria. The system often contains a model whose output can change between runs, and some expected answers need judgment. The result is a record of which cases passed, which failed and which did not finish. It is not one yes-or-no answer. These terms describe the parts of an evaluation:

passages.title: What is an evaluation, and how does it differ from a unit test?: A unit test checks code; an evaluation checks a task
passages.text: - A case is one input, its expected outcome and the criteria that decide success. Some guides call it a task or a test case. - A trial is one attempt at a case. A system whose output varies needs several trials of each case. - A grader decides whether a trial meets a criterion. It can be code, a person or another model. - A result record stores the verdict for each trial, together with what produced it: the case set and split, the system's versions, the grader and the run settings. Read repeated-trial results, quality, latency, cost, and coverage lists every field a report needs. Four kinds of check The checks around an AI feature fall into four kinds. Keep them separate, because each one answers a different question.

passages.title: What is an evaluation, and how does it differ from a unit test?: A unit test checks code; an evaluation checks a task
passages.text: - A unit check tests one function with a fixed input: blank text makes make_message raise ValueError. - A contract check tests a boundary between components. The model adapter is the code that sends a request to the model and reads the reply. A contract check can require that the reply is JSON, a structured text format, whose category is one of billing, delivery, account or other. The earlier lesson called this the output check. - An outcome check tests whether the task ended in the correct state: the message “I was charged twice” is filed as billing. The earlier lesson called this the task check. - A trajectory check tests the steps that a multi-step system took. An agent is a system that lets a model choose tool calls over several steps; its trajectory is the recorded sequence of those steps. A trajectory check can require that the agent looked up the order before it drafted a reply, and that it never called a refund tool.

passages.title: What is an evaluation, and how does it differ from a unit test?: A unit test checks code; an evaluation checks a task
passages.text: A unit check is an ordinary software test: the same input gives the same verdict on every run. A contract check gives the same verdict for the same output, but a model can return a different output on the next run, so an evaluation applies contract checks to every trial too. Outcome and trajectory checks are what an evaluation grades across its cases. A passing unit test suite tells you nothing about outcomes. A system's own statement, such as “I filed this as billing,” is not an outcome check either. The outcome check reads the stored category.

passages.title: What is an evaluation, and how does it differ from a unit test?: Follow one case through an evaluation run
passages.text: The figure follows one case. The dashed frame marks what the case supplies: an Input and an Expected result. The input goes to the System, which produces an Output. The output and the expected result both go to the Grader. The grader compares them and records one of three verdicts: pass, fail, or incomplete when the system produced no output to grade. The one thing to notice is where the expected result goes. It goes only to the grader. If the system could read it, the evaluation would measure copying, not the task. The evaluation repeats this path for every case in the set, and for several trials when the output can change between runs. The collection of result records is the evaluation result.

passages.title: What is an evaluation, and how does it differ from a unit test?: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Read each check below. Label it unit, contract, outcome or trajectory. One of them is none of the four; say what it actually checks. 1. The model adapter rejects a reply whose category field is "Billing!". 2. For each message in the case set, the grader compares the stored category with the expected category. 3. make_message(42) raises ValueError. 4. The agent's recorded steps show that it called the order-lookup tool before it drafted a reply. 5. The agent's final message says “I have updated your address,” and the check passes when that sentence is present. Check your understanding

passages.title: What is an evaluation, and how does it differ from a unit test?: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes An evaluation describes its own cases. If the case set contains no message about a closed account, the result says nothing about closed accounts. Every example in this series uses a handful of hand-written inbox cases run through keyword rules or a random stand-in. They show how each procedure works; they say nothing about how a real model handles real mail, and the later lessons do not repeat this point. The four kinds of check are a vocabulary for what each check proves; one test file can contain several kinds, as long as each check is labelled. Grade trajectories only for rules about the steps themselves, such as a required order or a forbidden tool. When several step sequences can reach the same correct outcome, a rigid trajectory check fails valid runs, so grade the outcome instead. Key takeaways - A unit test checks one code behavior and must pass every time. An evaluation grades a system across a set of cases and records each verdict. - Unit, contract, outcome and trajectory checks answer different questions. Passing one kind says nothing about the others. - A case carries its own expected result, and only the grader reads it. Best practices

passages.title: What is an evaluation, and how does it differ from a unit test?: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: - Record which kind of check produced each verdict, so a passing contract check is never reported as task success. - Check stored state for outcomes. Do not grade the system's description of what it did. References Official references checked October 20, 2026. - Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents — task, trial, grader, transcript and outcome definitions; grading outcomes rather than paths. - OpenAI: Evaluation best practices — why model output needs evaluations in addition to traditional software tests. - Python: unittest

passages.title: What is inference?: Inference uses existing model weights
passages.text: Inference means running a trained model on an input to obtain an output. Our support classifier receives a new message and produces category scores. A language model receives prepared text and generates a continuation. Both are inference. Ordinary inference uses existing learned weights. It does not retrain the model on the current message. An application can separately store messages or feed them into a later training process, so data retention and training policies still need checking. Follow one inbox request. The application accepts “My parcel has not arrived.” It prepares that text for the selected model. The execution software runs the model, obtains output scores, and returns a result. The application checks the output before presenting a suggestion. Preparing inputs and presenting results are parts of the overall request, not learned weight updates. Inference time is ambiguous unless someone states the measurement boundary. A user can wait for network transfer, a queue, loading a model into memory, input processing, output generation, and application work. A model's computation time may describe only part of that wait.

passages.title: What is inference?: Inference uses existing model weights
passages.text: A model can run in a process on your computer or on a remote machine. The meaning of inference stays the same. Serving means providing inference through a running system that accepts requests, for example a server with an HTTP interface. The lesson “Understand an HTTP client and server” explains HTTP and servers. This explains the name “inference server”: a program accepting requests to use a model. Downloading the model artifact is setup; training the model is learning; asking the loaded model to predict is inference.

passages.title: What is inference?: From new input to a checked result
passages.text: The first box is a new message: “My parcel has not arrived.” Inference runs the trained model on that message with the weights it already has and produces category scores. The application then checks those scores and shows a delivery suggestion. No arrow returns to the weights. Answering this message does not change the model; storing the message for a later training run would be a separate decision.

passages.title: What is inference?: Try it and check your understanding
passages.text: Classify these actions: download a model, update its weights on labelled messages, ask it to categorize a new message, save the answer in a database. Which one is inference? Check your understanding

passages.title: What is inference?: Limits, takeaways and references
passages.text: Limits and common mistakes Successful inference does not imply a correct answer. A server can return a well-formed prediction for an unsuitable input. Key takeaways - Inference runs a trained model on new input with its existing weights. Training is the step that changes the weights. - Downloading the model is setup. Serving makes inference available to callers through a running system. - When you report inference time, state which parts of the wait the measurement includes. References Official references checked October 18, 2026. - PyTorch: loading a model and running inference - Ollama: model inference API

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Problem
passages.text: The context budget manager fitted one kind of context: instructions, complete conversation turns and a question. An agent request has more parts. It also carries tool definitions, the tool calls the model made in this turn with their results, and passages that a retriever found. Each part has a different rule. The model cannot use a tool result without the call that produced it. A retrieved passage is data, but it can contain text that reads like an instruction. An old conversation turn may hold the decision that the question refers to. When the request is too large, one rule for every part loses the wrong thing. The naive approach concatenates everything in arrival order and removes the oldest messages until the request fits. On this build's fixture, that baseline removes messages. The first one is the system message, so the instructions and the tool definitions disappear. We will build assemble(request, count). It accepts six sections and a token allowance. It returns one request, its token count, and a trace that names every kept and dropped item with the reason. If the required sections cannot fit, it raises an error.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Problem
passages.text: Success check: on the supplied fixture, the request keeps the instructions in the system message, keeps the tool call with its result, keeps the PostgreSQL decision turn and the highest-ranked passage, and stays within input tokens. You need: Python 3.11 or later and a terminal. The build uses only the standard library. It downloads nothing and calls no model.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Concepts
passages.text: Six sections, two kinds A section is one source of context. This build has six: Section Example in the fixture Kind Instructions Answer from the conversation, the tool results and the evidence. Required Tool definitions search_docs(query) Required Current question Does the database we chose support row-level security? Required Tool calls and results call-1 and its result Required History Two complete turns from the budget build Optional Evidence Four passages with retrieval scores Optional Required sections always go into the request. If they do not fit, no selection of optional items can help, so the assembler rejects the request. Optional sections fill the space that remains. The model provider defines how tool calls look on the wire, not your application. This build uses the chat-completions layout: an assistant message carries tool_calls, and each result is a tool message whose tool_call_id matches the call. The OpenAI Python SDK types define these fields, with arguments as a JSON string. The Transformers tool-use guide also puts calls under tool_calls on an assistant message and results in tool messages, but its example tool message has no tool_call_id, and it expects arguments as a dictionary. The guide says to check each model card for the exact format. Convert at the adapter for your model; do not change the policy. Different sections need different selection rules

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Concepts
passages.text: History keeps the rule from the budget build: add complete turns from newest to oldest, and stop at the first turn that does not fit. Skipping a large recent turn to keep an older one could keep an answer that a later turn corrected. Evidence passages are independent of each other. A large passage that does not fit is skipped, and a smaller, lower-ranked passage may still fit. Passages are tried by score, highest first, with ties broken by ID so the result is repeatable. Fill order is a policy choice When both optional sections compete for the same space, the section filled first wins. fill_order makes that choice explicit. The default is history, then evidence. The fixture shows why the choice matters: with evidence first, the PostgreSQL decision turn no longer fits, and the question "the database we chose" has nothing to refer to. Evidence is data, not instructions Retrieved text can contain instructions. The fixture's wiki-note passage says to ignore the previous instructions. This is indirect prompt injection: instructions that arrive inside external content rather than from the user. OWASP LLM01:2025 lists separating untrusted content as a mitigation, and states that it is unclear whether any method prevents prompt injection completely.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Concepts
passages.text: The assembler does three things. It never places evidence in the system message. It wraps each passage in an <evidence> block inside the user message, after a note that says passages are not instructions. It escapes <, >, & and " in passage text, so a passage cannot close its own block and start a new one. Tool results are untrusted in the same way: a search tool can return text that someone else wrote. The assembler puts each result, unchanged, in its own tool message. Role separation is the only protection it applies to tool output; it does not escape or delimit it, because the chat template defines how a tool message is marked. A model can still follow an instruction that is inside a correctly escaped evidence block. The tests prove where the text goes, not how a model reacts to it. Keep tool authorization and permission checks outside the model request. Counts come from a stand-in counter The budget build counted with the pinned Gemma tokenizer. This build uses counter.py, a deterministic stand-in: each ASCII word is one piece, each other non-space character is one piece, and each message adds four pieces for role markers. Tool calls and tool definitions are counted as their JSON text.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Concepts
passages.text: These counts are not model token counts. They are stable, so the tests and the recorded trace are repeatable on any machine. Before you use the assembler with a real model, replace the counter with one that counts the final request your model server receives, including tool definitions.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Architecture
passages.text: The assembler is one function in one Python process. It has no HTTP server, store or model client. It reads a validated AssemblyRequest, calls the counter on complete candidate requests, and returns the request with its trace. The input is not changed. Every count is of the whole candidate request. The assembler never adds up separately counted pieces, because a chat template adds markers between messages and the pieces do not always add up to the total. The trace table above is the recorded output of the fixture. The required sections use tokens. The PostgreSQL decision turn adds . The long requirements turn would add , so it is dropped, and history stops. Then pg-rls fits, and the three other passages do not.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Working code
passages.text: Get the files Each file below is imported into this page from the downloadable example, so the page and the download cannot differ. Download assembler.py, contracts.py, counter.py, demo.py, request.json and test_assembler.py into one directory. The README lists the same files. Validate the request before counting parse_request turns JSON into frozen dataclasses. It rejects unknown fields, so a caller cannot send an images field that the counter would ignore. It rejects booleans where integers are expected, blank text, text longer than 16,384 characters, and non-finite scores. Tool exchanges get three extra checks. The tool must be declared. The arguments must include every required parameter and no unknown one. Call IDs must be unique, because a duplicate ID would make it unclear which result belongs to which call. The argument check covers names only. It does not check argument types or values. A real tool must validate its own arguments before it acts. Assemble the request build(passages, turns) renders a complete candidate request. The first count uses no optional items. If it is larger than the input budget, RequiredContextTooLarge carries both numbers so the caller can explain the rejection.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Working code
passages.text: add_history and add_evidence each count a candidate with one more item. add_history returns at the first turn that does not fit; add_evidence records the passage as dropped and continues. Both append a trace row for every item they consider, including turns older than a dropped turn, which are marked not tried. naive_truncate is the baseline. It puts the tool definitions into the system text, puts raw passages in front of the question, and removes messages from the front. audit checks any request for four structural problems: instructions missing from the system message, an assistant reply without its user message, a tool result without its call, and a call without its result. The stand-in counter Run the fixture The fixture reuses the two history turns from the budget build's request.json. It adds the search_docs tool, one call with its result, and four passages. Two passages paraphrase the PostgreSQL row security documentation; one is a long list of example policies; one contains an injected instruction. The allowance is tokens, with reserved for the answer and as a margin. From the directory with the files, run: demo.py assembles the fixture with the default order, again with evidence first, and runs the naive baseline. The recorded summary of the default assembly:

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Working code
passages.text: With evidence first, the same budget keeps and history turns. The injected passage now reaches the request, inside its escaped block, and the decision turn does not. The naive baseline uses tokens, and its audit reports instructions_in_system: .

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Failure cases
passages.text: Run the tests: The suite has tests. The first runs demo.py and compares its output with the recorded assembly-result.json. The others exercise these boundaries: Case Expected behavior

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Failure cases
passages.text: Required sections exceed the input budget Raise RequiredContextTooLarge with the required and available counts. Do not shorten a tool result. Required sections fit exactly Accept with zero unused tokens. One more output token makes the request fail. A tool result without its call, or a call to an undeclared tool Keep each call next to its result. Reject undeclared tools and duplicate call or passage IDs. Tool arguments that do not match the declared parameters Reject missing required arguments and unknown arguments. A passage contains instructions Keep it in the user message inside its evidence block. The system message stays exactly the instructions. A passage contains an evidence closing tag Escape it. The number of evidence blocks equals the number of kept passages. A high-ranked passage is too large Skip it and try the next passage. A recent turn is too large Stop adding history. Do not skip it to keep an older turn. Fill order starves a section History first keeps the decision turn; evidence first drops it. Oldest-first truncation The baseline loses the instructions; the assembler keeps them. Empty tools, history, tool results and evidence Accept. The request has a system message and a user message. Invalid numbers, unknown fields, blank text or oversized text Reject the request before counting.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Failure cases
passages.text: To check that the tests catch real defects, we removed three parts of the policy one at a time and ran the suite again. Without escaping, the closing-tag test fails. When history skips a large turn instead of stopping, the fixture test and the history test fail. When evidence stops at the first large passage instead of skipping it, the fixture test and the skip test fail. The tests check structure and size. They do not show that a model answers correctly from the assembled request, ignores the injected passage, or calls tools safely. Those need an evaluation with a real model and repeated trials.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Deployment
passages.text: Run it inside the application that calls the model The deployable unit is the three Python modules. Import parse_request and assemble in the process that sends requests to your model, and call them just before that call. The assembler holds no state between requests, so each worker can call it independently. Replace count_request with a counter for your model before deployment. Count the request in the exact form your model client sends, with the same chat template and tool definitions. If your client converts arguments from a JSON string to a dictionary, count after that conversion. Pass max_new_tokens from the result to the generation call. The number in the result does not limit generation by itself. Log the trace, not the text Log input_tokens, kept_turns, dropped_turns, the kept and dropped evidence IDs, and each RequiredContextTooLarge with its two counts. Do not log message or passage text: it can contain user data. A rise in dropped decision turns or in required-context rejections is a reason to review the budget or the fill order. To roll back a policy change, keep the previous module version and its recorded fixture together. A changed fill_order default is a behavior change; run the fixture test and compare the trace before you switch.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Scaling
passages.text: Where the work grows Each candidate count renders and counts the whole request again. With h history turns and e passages, one assembly makes up to 1 + h + e counter calls, and each call processes the full candidate. The budget build measured this cost with a real tokenizer and showed that it grows faster than the history. The same cost applies here, plus the size of tool definitions, which every count includes. This build records no timing. The stand-in counter is much faster than a real tokenizer, so timing it would not predict production cost. Measure with your real counter, your largest tool set and a realistic number of passages. Changes for larger requests A first change is to count the complete request once and return at once when everything fits. A second is to cap the number of passages the retriever sends, since passages beyond the budget are only counted to be dropped. Caching counts for unchanged parts needs care: a template may add different markers at section boundaries, so test that cached part counts add up to the full count before you rely on them.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Key takeaways
passages.text: - Split context into required and optional sections. Reject the request when required sections do not fit; do not truncate them. - Use a selection rule that matches each section: stop at the first history turn that does not fit, but skip a passage that does not fit. - Fill order decides which optional section wins when space is short. Make it a named setting and test it with questions that depend on each section. - Keep a tool call and its result together, and keep retrieved text out of the system message, inside escaped blocks.

passages.title: Build a context assembler for instructions, history, tools, and evidence: Best practices
passages.text: - Count the whole candidate request with your model's own tokenizer and template; the stand-in counter is for tests only. - Return a trace that names each dropped item and the reason, and log the trace without the text. - Write a failure test for each rule, and check that the test fails when you remove the rule. - Validate tool arguments again inside each tool. The assembler checks names, not values.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Before you build
passages.text: An LLM application has two separate jobs: prepare a request and ask a model to generate a response. The model does not automatically remember the messages stored in your application. For a plain chat request, your application sends the history it wants the model to see. Consider a support chat. The application sends an instruction—“Answer from the conversation”—and a user question. On the next request, it may send that instruction again, the earlier question and answer, and the new question. Repeating this process makes the input grow. A message holds a role and content: system instructions, user text, or an assistant response. A tokenizer converts the rendered conversation into units the model processes. A context window limits the sequence the model can handle. The input must leave space for the tokens the model generates next. The request follows this path: 1. Your Python application assembles instructions, conversation history, and the latest question. 2. A budgeting function selects a history that fits while reserving room for the answer. 3. A model server would process the selected request and generate a response. 4. Your application would store the response for a later turn. This build implements step 2 and tests its boundary. It stops before generation, so you can inspect exactly what survives without downloading model weights or paying for API calls.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Before you build
passages.text: FastAPI makes the same budgeting function callable over HTTP. LangChain and Google ADK provide other places to integrate it. None changes the underlying policy: keep the instructions and latest question, retain complete recent turns, and reject requests whose required text cannot fit. Before continuing: you should be able to identify the model, the model server, and your application as separate components. You should also be able to explain why storing a message in a database does not mean it is present in the next model request.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Problem
passages.text: A chat application keeps appending messages to a conversation. Eventually, it sends more text than the model can accept—or uses the entire input allowance and leaves no room for an answer. Removing the first few messages sounds sufficient until the application removes its instructions, keeps an answer without its question, or forgets a decision the user expects it to remember. We will build a context budget manager that makes those choices explicit. It accepts instructions, completed conversation turns, a new question, and a token allowance. It returns the selected messages, their token count, and how many turns it removed. If the required text cannot fit, it returns an error. You need: Python functions and lists, basic JSON, and a terminal. Everything in this article runs on a CPU. The setup downloads tokenizer files once; it does not download model weights, need an API key, or generate an answer. The stack and the boundary Responsibility Choice Why it is here

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Concepts
passages.text: Count the request the model actually receives A token is a unit produced by the model’s tokenizer. Counting words, characters, or bytes does not tell us the token count reliably across code, languages, and punctuation. The input is also more than the visible message text. The chat template adds role boundaries and an assistant prefix. We call apply_chat_template(..., tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True) so those tokens are included. Transformers chat templates This count is exact for this pinned text serialization. It is not a promise about a different inference server that inserts instructions, changes the template, or adds tool definitions. Count after those additions, or use that server’s own counting interface. A model limit and an application budget are different A context window is the model’s capacity for the sequence it processes. Your application can choose a smaller limit to bound work and keep requests predictable. This service permits an application limit up to 8,192 tokens. The example fixture deliberately uses just 512 so trimming is easy to inspect. From that allowance we reserve 128 tokens for generation and 32 for a margin. That leaves 352 for the rendered input. The margin is a deliberate buffer, not a replacement for counting the correct template. A larger reserve may improve the chance of a complete answer, but reduces the history we can send.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Concepts
passages.text: The generation caller must actually pass the returned max_new_tokens limit. A number in a budget report cannot constrain a separate model server on its own. This project stops before that invocation. Preserve complete turns, then admit the loss A turn here is one user message and its completed assistant reply. Required instructions and the current question always stay. We try adding completed turns from newest to oldest and stop as soon as the next pair does not fit. Why stop instead of skipping a large recent turn and inserting a smaller old one? The old message might contain a decision that the newer one corrected. Keeping a continuous tail of the conversation makes the selection rule easier to reason about. It still does not preserve every useful fact. A request can fit perfectly and still lack the fact needed to answer it. The manager reports dropped turns; it does not summarize them, retrieve them later, or prove that the retained messages are sufficient.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Architecture
passages.text: Components The core takes a validated BudgetRequest and a callable that counts messages. It has no dependency on FastAPI, Transformers, LangChain, or ADK. Pydantic defines the shared data contract; the tokenizer adapter supplies the model-specific serialization. The service holds one tokenizer per worker. Conversation state arrives with each request and is not stored. In a real application, trusted instructions should come from server configuration; a public client should not choose the system policy by sending this internal request format. Request flow The current question is never shortened automatically. A pasted document that makes the required text too large produces a specific failure. The caller must reduce the document, retrieve relevant passages, or change its approved budget and retry. Repeating the same request cannot solve that failure. Before and after Our fixture has a long requirements discussion followed by a short decision to use PostgreSQL. The new question asks which database was chosen. The manager removes the requirements discussion and retains the decision. This demonstrates what remains available to a future model call; it does not demonstrate generated-answer quality.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Working code
passages.text: Each history item must contain both user and assistant. The service accepts at most 64 completed turns, 16,384 characters per message, and 65,536 characters across the request. These are application limits for this example, not model capabilities. They bound tokenization work before counting begins. extra='forbid' is important: a caller cannot send a tools or images field and receive a misleading count that silently excludes it. Strict integers also prevent a boolean or a numeric string from being accepted as a token budget. These checks apply to direct Python calls as well as HTTP requests. The character limits are resource limits, not an alternative token-counting method. An HTTP gateway must also cap the raw body before the application parses JSON. Implement the policy The first count contains only the required messages. If it is already too large, no history policy can make it fit. RequiredContextTooLarge carries the required and available counts so the caller can explain the rejection. The loop builds a candidate from one older pair plus the turns already kept. It counts the entire candidate with the real template. It never subtracts a guessed number of tokens per message. The result is restored to chronological order because each older pair is inserted before the retained tail.

Template processing may normalize whitespace; the count describes that rendered input. The counters in the result let callers display a “conversation shortened” notice and track how often this happens. This implementation favors an inspectable policy over minimizing tokenizer calls. The scaling measurements below show the cost of repeatedly counting a growing candidate. Supply the Gemma counter There are two separate safeguards here. The model revision fixes the download, while the file hashes catch a changed local tokenizer or template. The service refuses to start if those checks fail. Changing models means supplying a new adapter and rerunning the budget and serialization tests; changing only a model-name string is insufficient. add_generation_prompt=True counts the prefix that starts the next assistant response. enable_thinking=False fixes the selected Gemma mode. If a caller enables thinking or adds content afterward, it must recount the resulting request and reserve output for that mode. Expose the same function with FastAPI Startup loads the tokenizer before the app becomes ready. /health reports the revision and template hash. /budget delegates to the core and turns an oversized required context into HTTP 422. Invalid schemas also return 422, without echoing conversation content in the error response.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Failure cases
passages.text: Run the actual tokenizer and HTTP tests: The supplied suite passes 27 tests, including parameterized cases. They exercise these boundaries: Case Expected behavior Required text alone exceeds the input budget Reject; keep the original text intact. HTTP returns required_context_too_large. Required text fits exactly Accept with zero unused input space. Reserving one more output token makes it fail. A recent turn is too large Stop; do not skip it to recover older conversation. A history item lacks an assistant reply Reject the incomplete turn. Empty history Accept; instructions and the current question still count. Empty or whitespace-only messages Reject invalid input. Chinese, Arabic, emoji, and multiline text Count with the tokenizer and preserve the selected source text. Tools, images, oversized fields, or invalid numeric settings Reject the unsupported request shape or resource limit. A tokenizer file is missing or changed Fail startup rather than serve counts under the wrong profile. An old fact exists only in a removed turn Report the removed turn; the fact is absent from the returned messages.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Failure cases
passages.text: The last test matters as much as the overflow tests. It inserts a project label into the discarded turn and checks that the selected messages no longer contain it. Passing that test proves the information was removed. It does not prove a model will admit the loss when asked about it. Test questions that depend on early decisions, corrections, pronouns, and details spread across several turns. Measure answer quality after trimming when you add generation. Preserving complete turns avoids broken pairs, but a recent answer can still refer to an older fact that was removed. A context budget also does not sanitize prompt injection or literal model control tokens. This example assumes ordinary text messages from the application. Keep tool authorization, untrusted-content handling, and access checks outside this counter; never treat a successful budget result as a security decision.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Scaling
passages.text: Measure before adding workers Run the included benchmark: It warms the tokenizer, then runs 30 sequential calls per case. Each completed turn repeats two short English sentences ten times each. The application limit is 8,192, the output reserve is 1,024, and the margin is 64. Every turn fits in this workload, exposing the cost of repeatedly counting larger candidates. Measured on an Apple M4 Pro, 14 CPU cores, 48 GB RAM, macOS 27.0.1, Python 3.11.11 with Transformers 5.20.1. Timings exclude startup, HTTP, schema construction, and model generation. The p95 is the 29th sorted observation out of 30; this small sample describes this local run only. The benchmark source and recorded result are included. This is not an HTTP throughput test. The 64-turn result is a reason to improve the algorithm before placing it on a latency-sensitive request path. Where the work grows The newest turn is tokenized again whenever we try adding an older one. If many turns fit, we keep processing the same text. Doubling the history can therefore cost much more than twice as much. More FastAPI workers do not remove that repeated work.

passages.title: Build a context budget manager: Scaling
passages.text: A first optimization is to count the full conversation once and return immediately when it fits. Measure this against both short conversations and requests that overflow. For long overflowing histories, consider cached serialized segments or a search over possible cut points. Before using either, test how the exact template handles boundaries, normalization, and conversation-dependent content. Do not assume that separately tokenized pieces always add up to the full request count. Cache keys need the tokenizer revision, template hash, role, and content. In a multi-tenant application, also account for isolation, sensitive content, eviction, and invalidation. The current example has no cross-request cache. Separate budgeting from inference capacity This service spends CPU time on validation, template rendering, and tokenization. It loads no model weights and allocates no model KV cache. A later inference service has separate limits for model memory, cached attention state, concurrent generations, and output lengths. Test that service with its real runtime and hardware. The model’s advertised context capacity is not evidence that your VPS can serve that many tokens concurrently. Keep the configured inference limit aligned with the manager, and measure queue time, peak memory, time to first token, and complete-request latency separately.
