passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Problem
passages.text: You have a collection of notes and want to find the one that helps with a question. A program needs a rule for choosing which note to show first. Matching a word is a start, but a common word such as “a” can also match an unrelated note. A retriever selects documents from a collection in response to a query, the text someone searches for. In this build, each document is one short passage. The output is a ranked list: the passages with the highest similarity scores come first. We’ll build a command-line retriever in Python. It counts shared words, gives more weight to words found in fewer documents, and compares the resulting numbers. The supplied collection has three passages so you can follow every calculation before working with a larger collection. By the end, you will have a runnable script that accepts a query and prints a score beside each passage. You will check a useful match, inspect a misleading match, and test what happens when the query shares no words with the collection. Those checks establish how this implementation behaves; a real search application also needs evaluation against questions its users ask.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Concepts
passages.text: A document is one stored text the retriever can return, and a query is the text a person searches with. A document is relevant when it helps answer that query; the retriever cannot see relevance directly, so it estimates it from shared words. The retriever turns words into numbers so it can compare a query with each document. Five terms describe that process: TokenA unit extracted from text. This tokenizer lowercases text and extracts sequences of ASCII letters as words. That is simpler than a language model's tokenizer in What are tokens and tokenizers?, which splits text into subword pieces with numeric IDs. VocabularyThe distinct words found in the documents, sorted into a fixed order. A query cannot add words to that order. TF-IDF weightTerm frequency (TF) counts occurrences of a word. Inverse document frequency (IDF) gives less weight to words found in many documents. Multiplying them produces the weight used here. VectorAn ordered list of numbers, with one weight per vocabulary word. An absent word has weight zero. Query and document vectors use the same word order. Cosine similarityA comparison of two vectors that accounts for their lengths. Shared words contribute to the score. A high score alone does not mean that a passage answers the question.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Concepts
passages.text: For example, a search for weights memory bits should put the passage about reducing model memory first. The program only compares the words: you can inspect the search behavior without knowing how model compression works.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Architecture
passages.text: rank(query, documents) runs in one Python process. The documents live in a list in the source file. Each call rebuilds the vocabulary and word weights, scores every document, and returns sorted (score, document) pairs. There is no database or network call. The documents define the vocabulary. The query must use the same vocabulary and weights so that each coordinate refers to the same word. Unknown query words are ignored. Keep preparation and scoring in one function so you can trace the whole request. This also means repeated requests redo the same preparation. The scaling section separates those two responsibilities. The figure shows selected word weights from the supplied example. The next section constructs those weights and calculates the resulting similarity score.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Working code
passages.text: Runtime: Python 3.10 or newer. Dependencies: Python standard library only. Save this as retrieve.py. You can also download the same Python file. tokens() lowercases text and keeps sequences of ASCII letters. Counter counts each word. The idf dictionary assigns a weight to every word in the document vocabulary; vector() applies those weights to document and query counts. cosine() compares two vectors and returns zero when either has zero length. Finally, rank() sorts all scores from highest to lowest. The score measures word-based similarity, not the probability that a document answers the question. Run the example: Expected output with the supplied documents: Trace the intermediate state Follow the same query, retrieval documents query, through the supplied corpus:

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Working code
passages.text: 1. Normalization produces ["retrieval", "documents", "query"]. The three documents define a sorted vocabulary of 23 terms; the query cannot add new coordinates. 2. Each query term occurs once and appears in only one document. In this implementation, each therefore receives weight 1.693147181. The query has three nonzero coordinates; the other 20 are zero. 3. The first document has seven terms. Six have that same weight; a receives 1.287682072 because it occurs in two documents. The document and query must use the same vocabulary order and weights. Equal vector lengths alone do not show that alignment. 4. Comparing the query against that document gives 0.675305842 before display rounding. The other two documents share no query terms and score 0.000. The CLI prints all three rows; the caller still has to decide whether any result is useful. Calculate the score This implementation uses smoothed IDF. Let N be the number of documents and df the number containing a word. Its IDF is 1 + ln((1 + N) / (1 + df)), where ln is the natural logarithm, implemented by Python's math.log. Multiply that value by the word's occurrence count to obtain its vector weight. The added ones are part of this chosen formula; other TF-IDF implementations can use different conventions. The scikit-learn reference describes this smoothing formula.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Working code
passages.text: There are three documents. A query word found in one document receives 1 + ln(4 / 2), approximately 1.693147181. The word a appears in two documents, so it receives 1 + ln(4 / 3), approximately 1.287682072. In this example, each of those words occurs once per relevant text, so its occurrence count does not change the weight. To calculate cosine similarity, first multiply weights at matching positions and add the products. This is the dot product. The query shares three words with the first document, giving 3 × 1.693147181², approximately 8.600242125. Positions where either weight is zero contribute nothing. Next, calculate each vector's length: square its weights, add those squares, and take the square root. The query has three nonzero weights, giving length 2.932616941. The first document has six weights of approximately 1.693147181 and one of approximately 1.287682072, giving length 4.342650040. Divide the dot product by the product of those lengths: 8.600242125 / (2.932616941 × 4.342650040) is approximately 0.675305842. The CLI rounds it to 0.675. The code uses full-precision values; the numbers here are rounded for display. The other two documents share no query words, so their dot products and scores are zero.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Working code
passages.text: There is no posting list or persistent index here: rank() rebuilds dense coordinates on every call. A BM25 index would be a different implementation, with its own tests. This build does not implement term-frequency saturation or BM25 document-length normalization. Download retrieve_trace.py beside retrieve.py, then run python3 retrieve_trace.py. It records the tokenizer output, vocabulary, sparse representations of the query and first document, and the actual rank() results. The sparse view omits zero coordinates for readability; the retriever itself still constructs dense vectors.

Ties keep the original document order. Taking the first result without checking its score would present an arbitrary passage as evidence. The command-line entry point substitutes a default query when its arguments are empty. That differs from calling rank("", DOCUMENTS) directly. Test the function and the interface separately. A positive score is not enough either: the neural-network query matches the word “a” in unrelated passages. Keep that query as a known failure when evaluating changes. The tokenizer also drops digits and non-ASCII letters. Word order is lost, and synonyms do not match automatically. passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Deployment
passages.text: This example deploys as a command-line program. Copy retrieve.py to a directory owned by your user on the VPS. From that directory, check the interpreter and run a smoke test: Use Python 3.10 or newer. The quantization passage should be first. No package installation, API key, listening port, or persistent process is required. Run the regression checks above on the VPS too. Keep a versioned copy of the script and its documents. For this CLI, a release replaces the file for subsequent invocations; rollback restores the previous file. There is no index file or database migration to coordinate yet. The example has no HTTP server, authentication, request limits, or concurrency controls. A service needs those boundaries, plus request validation, timeouts, and a defined no-match response. Running this file on a VPS does not provide them. In a service, load documents from a controlled source rather than accepting a whole corpus with every request. Record request duration, document count, errors, and no-match outcomes. Avoid logging raw queries or document contents by default because they may contain private data.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Scaling
passages.text: The code favors readability. It rebuilds word counts and weights for every query, creates a dense vector for each comparison, then sorts every result. Adding web workers would repeat this work and multiply the memory used for the document collection. The current implementation does not keep an entire dense document matrix in memory. It constructs one document vector at a time. Word counts, vocabulary, query vector, and the full result list remain resident during ranking. Cost in this code What changes as the collection grows Next implementation change Rebuilding counts and word weights Preparation is repeated for every query Build an index once per document version Checking every document for every vocabulary word More documents and unique words increase preparation time Compute document frequencies while indexing Creating and comparing dense vectors Work grows with both documents and vocabulary size Store sparse weights and score matching documents through an inverted index Sorting every score Work and the result list grow with document count Select only the required top results, then sort that subset When indexing is separate, publish a version containing the vocabulary, word weights, and document representations together. A query must not use weights from one version against vectors built with another. Build a replacement index before switching requests to it, and retain the previous version for rollback.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Scaling
passages.text: Measure before choosing a larger service. Use a fixed collection and query set, record the hardware and Python version, and measure preparation time, query latency, memory, and retrieval quality separately. For an HTTP service, also test concurrent requests and report tail latency, not just an average. No throughput or production capacity is claimed for this example. A useful next experiment is to increase document count and vocabulary size independently, then compare the current function with an index reused across queries.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Key takeaways
passages.text: - A score is meaningful only with the vocabulary, weighting and document version that produced it. Two equal-length vectors can still refer to different terms. - Zero scores establish no shared vocabulary here. Positive scores still admit irrelevant common-word matches, as the neural-network question demonstrates. - Reusing preparation requires an explicit index version. Adding workers to this function alone repeats preparation and duplicates corpus memory.

passages.title: Build a text retriever and understand every score: Best practices
passages.text: - Preserve known bad queries in the evaluation set. A tokenizer change should be checked against useful matches, no matches and false positives together. - Define no-match and empty-input behavior at the application boundary. The CLI prints zero scores and substitutes a default query; those are interface choices, not search-quality guarantees. - Measure preparation, scoring, memory and quality separately on a fixed workload before adopting an index or claiming a capacity limit.

passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Problem
passages.text: The context budget manager removes old turns when a conversation no longer fits, and it reports how many it removed. A decision made early in a long conversation disappears with its turn. The next request cannot use it. Compaction replaces removed turns with a shorter record of what they said. It sounds like a fix, but a shorter record can also drop facts, keep facts that a later turn replaced, or change their wording. You cannot see those losses by reading the token count. This build compacts removed turns into cited notes and then tests the result. A probe names one fact from the conversation. After compaction, each probe reports whether its fact reached the request. On the supplied fixture, the drop-oldest policy from the budget build keeps of probed facts. The compactor keeps , loses , and keeps decision that a later turn replaced. The build's job is to make all three numbers visible. Success check: the recorded probe report matches a fresh run, every note quotes its cited turn word for word, and each known loss is reported by a named test. You need: Python 3.11 or later and a terminal. The build uses only the standard library and calls no model.

passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Concepts
passages.text: Compaction keeps a record, not the conversation The compactor works in two parts. Recent complete turns stay as they are, exactly as in the budget build. Turns that do not fit pass through an extractor, a function that turns removed turns into notes. The notes go into the request in the space that is left. This build's extractor is a keyword rule. It splits each removed message into sentences and keeps a sentence when it contains a cue word: must, chose, will use, decided, deadline or one of the others in CUES. Each note records its turn number and role, so a reader can check it against the original conversation. A model-written summary is another extractor. It can paraphrase and combine sentences, and it can also leave out or change facts. This build does not include one. The extractor argument is where you would plug it in, and the same probes would test it. A probe checks one fact by exact text A probe has an ID, a kind (decision, constraint or detail) and the exact text of the fact. After compaction, the probe report looks for that text in the final messages: Status Meaning

passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Concepts
passages.text: preserved The fact is in the request. lost The fact is not in the request. stale The fact was replaced by a later turn, and it is still in the request. absent The fact was replaced, and it is not in the request. Exact matching suits an extractor that copies sentences. It is too strict for a summarizer that paraphrases: a correct paraphrase would count as lost. If you add a summarizer, you need a matching method that accepts paraphrases, and a human review of that method. Stale is worse than lost A lost fact leaves a gap that a careful model can report. A stale fact gives the model a wrong answer to repeat. In the fixture, turn 2 says the first version will use MySQL. Turn 5 chooses PostgreSQL and explains that it replaces MySQL. The extractor keeps the turn 2 sentence because it contains will use. It keeps the first sentence of turn 5 because it contains chose. It drops the second sentence of turn 5, the one that says PostgreSQL replaces MySQL, because that sentence has no cue word. The notes now hold both database decisions and nothing that says which one is current. The turn numbers give an order, but nothing in the notes says that the later decision cancels the earlier one.

passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Concepts
passages.text: A preserved fact can still be ignored or misread by a model. A probe report tells you what a model could see. To learn what it answers, run the compacted request through a model on a fixed set of questions and grade the answers.

passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Architecture
passages.text: The compactor is one function in one Python process. It reads a validated CompactionRequest, calls the counter on whole candidate requests, and returns the request, the notes and the notes that did not fit. probe_report is a separate function; it reads only the final messages and the probe list. Notes go into the current user message inside a <notes> block, after a line that says they quote the conversation and are not instructions. They never go into the system message: the text came from users and assistants, and moving it into the system message would give it the weight of an instruction. This follows the rule the context assembler uses for evidence. The notes_reserve setting keeps space for notes before recent turns fill the budget. Without it, a long recent history would leave no space for notes at all.

It then keeps recent complete turns inside available - notes_reserve and stops at the first turn that does not fit. The extractor runs only on removed turns. Notes from turns that are still in the request would repeat them. The notes are added newest first, and the loop stops at the first note that does not fit. Notes from the oldest turns are dropped first, and dropped_notes returns them so the caller can log the loss. escape replaces <, > and & in note text. A sentence that contains </notes> cannot close the block early. drop_oldest is the baseline. passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Failure cases
passages.text: The stale and lost results are not bugs to hide. They are the measured limits of a keyword extractor. A change to the extractor should change the probe report, and the recorded result makes that change visible in review.

passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Deployment
passages.text: Run compaction where the request is built The deployable unit is compactor.py with a counter for your model. Call compact in the process that sends model requests, after you load the conversation and before you call the model. It keeps no state; the full conversation stays in your application's store, and only the outgoing request is compacted. Replace count_request with a counter for your model before deployment, and pass max_new_tokens to the generation call yourself. Keep the probes with the release Treat probes.json as part of the release. Before you change the cue list, the notes reserve or the extractor, run the probes on the fixture and on a sample of real conversations with facts you have labeled. Compare the new probe report with the recorded one. Roll back by restoring the previous extractor and its recorded report together. In production, log removed_turns, the number of notes, dropped_notes and the request size. Do not log note text: it quotes the user. No server deployment or model call was made for this build. The tests ran on Python 3.11.11 and 3.15.0 on macOS.

passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Scaling
passages.text: Where the work grows compact counts one candidate per recent turn and one per note, and each count processes the whole request. Extraction is one regular-expression pass over the removed text. With a real tokenizer, counting dominates; the budget build measured that cost. This build records no timing, because the stand-in counter would not predict it. Recompacting the whole history on every request repeats work. A common change is to store notes for each removed turn once and reuse them. Stored notes must be invalidated when the extractor or the cue list changes, and they must keep their turn citations. Probes scale with labeling, not with code The probe runner is cheap. The expensive part is writing probes: each one needs a person to name the fact and say which later turn, if any, replaced it. probes on one conversation show how this extractor fails. They do not estimate how often it fails on your conversations. For that, label facts in a sample of real conversations, keep the sample fixed, and report lost and stale counts for each change.

passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Key takeaways
passages.text: - Compaction trades tokens for information. Measure the trade with named facts, not with the token count. - Report three outcomes: preserved, lost and stale. A stale fact can produce a confident wrong answer. - A keyword extractor keeps cued sentences word for word and with citations, but it loses facts without cue words and cannot tell that a decision was replaced. - Keep compacted notes out of the system message, inside an escaped block.

passages.title: Build context compaction with information-loss tests: Best practices
passages.text: - Write probes from the conversation before you run the compactor, including facts you expect it to miss. - Cite the source turn for every note so a reviewer can check it. - Return dropped notes and log their count; do not drop them silently. - Test any summarizer you add with the same probes, and add a review step for paraphrase matching.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Problem
passages.text: An assistant that remembers things keeps them somewhere: user preferences, notes for the current task, an agent's working drafts. When the application builds the next request, it selects items from that store. If the store is one shared list, the selection decides what each user sees. A shared list fails in a quiet way. Bob asks about the export job. A word-overlap ranking returns the three items that share the most words with the question, and one of them belongs to Alice. In this build's fixture, the naive baseline returns at least one other user's item in all recorded queries. Nothing crashes; the request just contains data Bob must never see. Agents add two more boundaries. A task's notes should not follow the user into a different task. A sub-agent that searches documentation does not need the planner's drafts or the user's preferences, and it should not get the planner's tools. We will build a scoped context store. Every item has a scope, the requester is a (user, task, agent) principal, and the store returns only the items that principal may read. A sub-agent gets an explicit handoff. The tests check each boundary and show the baseline's leaks.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Problem
passages.text: Success check: in the recorded scenario, no principal receives another user's item, a new task does not see the previous task's notes, and the researcher receives only the handoff. You need: Python 3.11 or later and a terminal. The build uses only the standard library, keeps everything in memory and calls no model.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Concepts
passages.text: Four scopes A scope says who may read an item. This build uses four: Scope Who may read it Example in the fixture app Every principal. Written only from configuration. The answer policy user The same user, in any task Bob prefers short answers. task The same user in the same task Task 17: move the export job to PostgreSQL. agent The same user, task and agent The planner's draft question A principal is the requester: one user, one task and one agent. The store compares an item's scope keys with the principal's. A task item matches only when both the user and the task match, so the check never relies on task IDs being unique across users. Scope keys come from the principal When the planner writes an item, the store fills the item's user, task and agent from the principal. The caller cannot supply them. A note whose text says user_id: alice is still Bob's note. This rule is what makes the other rules hold: if a caller could set an item's owner, the read check would protect nothing. Principals cannot write app items. Application policy comes from configuration, so a user cannot add an instruction that every other user would receive. Agents read declared scopes and get declared tools

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Concepts
passages.text: Each agent declares the scopes it reads and the tools it receives. The fixture's planner reads all four scopes and gets search_docs and delegate. The researcher reads only app and its own agent scope, and gets only search_docs. OWASP LLM06:2025 recommends limiting the tools an agent can call to the minimum necessary. The store enforces one tool rule itself: only an agent with the delegate tool can call handoff. For every other tool, build_context returns the agent's tool list, and the application that executes tool calls must refuse any call to a tool that is not on that list. This build does not execute tools, so it does not enforce that part. A handoff is an explicit copy The planner does not share its context with the researcher. It calls handoff with a brief and a list of item IDs. The store checks that the planner has the delegate tool and can read each item, then copies the brief and the items into the researcher's agent scope, with their source recorded. The researcher sees what it was given and nothing else.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Concepts
passages.text: A handoff is all or nothing. The store validates every copy before it writes any, so a failed handoff leaves the store and its version unchanged. Each handoff gets the next number for that user, and its items are named handoff-<n>-brief and handoff-<n>-item-<k>, so a second handoff in the same task does not collide with the first. Caller-written IDs cannot start with handoff-, so a written item can never take a number a later handoff needs. The store trusts the principal it receives. Your application must authenticate the user before it builds a principal. A scope also says nothing about whether the content is safe to show: an item written into Bob's scope that contains Alice's data will reach Bob. Check document permissions before content is written into a scope.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Architecture
passages.text: The store is one in-memory object in one Python process. write, configure, handoff and close_task change it; each change increases its version. visible filters items for a principal. build_context turns the visible items into a request: app items and the agent's role go into the system message, and the other items go into the user message inside escaped <item> blocks. The table above is the recorded output of the fixture scenario. Every query asks the same question, so differences come from scope rules, not from the question. After close_task, Bob's task 17 has only the app policy and his user preference left. The naive list still returns Alice's items. ContextCache reuses a built context only for the same principal, question and store version. A cache keyed only by the question would return Bob's context to Alice.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Working code
passages.text: Get the files Download isolation.py, demo.py, scenario.json and test_isolation.py into one directory. The README lists them. The store The read rule has two parts. Item.visible_to compares scope keys: it returns early for app items, then requires a matching user, then a matching task, then a matching agent. Each check narrows the previous one. ContextStore.visible then keeps only the scopes the requesting agent declares in reads, which is how the researcher is kept away from user and task items. Principal and Agent validate themselves when they are created. IDs must be lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, so a blank or None user cannot become a wildcard. An agent must read its own agent scope; otherwise a handoff would be invisible to it. write checks item IDs for duplicates only among app items and the writer's own items. A global check would answer "duplicate" when another user already has that ID, which tells the writer that the other user's item exists. naive_context is the baseline: it ranks every item in the store by words shared with the question and takes the top three. The scenario

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Failure cases
passages.text: Another user's item matches the question The scoped store never returns it. The naive list returns it in every recorded query. The same user starts a new task The new task sees app and user items only. One agent's scratch notes Other agents in the same task cannot read them. A sub-agent needs part of the parent's context It receives the brief and the chosen items, and only its own tools. A handoff names an item the sender cannot read Reject the handoff. A handoff fails partway Validate every copy first; a failed handoff writes nothing and leaves the version unchanged. A second handoff in the same task Number it; its items do not collide with the first handoff's. An agent without the delegate tool hands off Reject the handoff. A caller writes an ID that starts with handoff- Reject the write; that prefix is reserved for handoffs. Item text or a payload claims another user's scope Take scope keys from the principal. Reject writes to the app scope. An item ID that another user already uses Accept it. Only the writer's own duplicate is rejected. A task is closed Remove its task and agent items. Other users' items remain. A cached context for another principal or an older store Miss the cache and build a new context. Item text contains an item closing tag Escape it. The number of closing tags equals the number of scoped items. Invalid principals and unknown agents Reject blank, uppercase, None or space-containing IDs and unconfigured agents.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Failure cases
passages.text: To check that the tests catch real defects, we removed parts of the rules one at a time. Without the task check, the task-boundary test and the fixture test fail. With a cache key that ignores the principal, the cache test fails. Without escaping, the closing-tag test fails. When write stores no user key, almost every test fails. These tests check what the store returns. They do not test a model: a model can still repeat whatever is in its request, and isolation cannot protect data that was written into the wrong scope.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Deployment
passages.text: From memory to a real store The deployable logic is Item.visible_to, the write rule and the handoff. The in-memory list is for the lesson. In a real application, store items in a database table with scope, user_id, task_id and agent_id columns, and put the scope conditions in every query that reads items. Filtering after a broad query works too, but a missing filter then leaks every row. Build the principal from your authenticated session, never from request fields that a client controls. Give each agent its tool list and readable scopes from configuration. Deletion, logs and rollback close_task deletes task and agent items in memory. A real store must also delete or invalidate cached contexts, search indexes and copies made by handoffs. Test deletion end to end: write an item, close the task, then search every place the item could appear. Log principal IDs, item IDs and counts of visible items. Do not log item text. To roll back a scope-rule change, restore the previous code and run the scenario test before you switch; a change in visible_items is a behavior change. No database, server deployment or model call was made for this build. The tests ran on Python 3.11.11 and 3.15.0 on macOS.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Scaling
passages.text: Where the work grows visible scans every item in the store, so each request costs time in proportion to the total number of items. That is acceptable for a lesson and wrong for a shared service. A database index on (user_id, task_id, agent_id) lets each query read only the principal's rows. This build records no timing; measure with your store and your item counts. The cache keys on the store version, which changes on every write by any user. With many users, Bob's cache would miss whenever Alice writes. A per-principal version, increased only by writes that principal can read, keeps hits without crossing users. Test it with the same cross-user cache case. More agents and more tasks Handoffs copy items, so storage grows with the number of handoffs. Copies are simple to reason about, and deleting a task removes them. If copies become too large, store references instead, and check at read time that the receiver may still read each referenced item.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Key takeaways
passages.text: - Give every context item a scope and derive its visibility from the requesting user, task and agent. - Take scope keys from the principal, never from the payload or the text. - Hand a sub-agent a brief and chosen items, and give it only the tools it needs. - Key caches and deletion by scope too; a leak through a cache is still a leak.

passages.title: Build isolated contexts for users, tasks, and agents: Best practices
passages.text: - Authenticate before you build a principal, and check document permissions before content is written into a scope. - Write a cross-user test for every read path: direct reads, caches, search and handoffs. - Make duplicate checks and error messages per user, so errors do not reveal other users' data. - Keep scope conditions in the database query, not only in application code after the query.

passages.title: Compare context-selection strategies on a fixed evaluation set: Problem
passages.text: The earlier builds in this series each choose context with one rule. The context budget manager keeps the newest complete turns. Context compaction adds cue-word notes from removed turns. A retriever-style rule would keep the turns that share words with the question. Which one should an application use? One example cannot answer that. Each rule wins on a conversation that suits it and fails on one that does not. Comparing them needs a fixed evaluation set: the same cases, the same budget, the same counter and the same grader for every strategy, with the per-case results kept, not only the totals. We will build that comparison. strategies.py holds four selection strategies. evaluate.py loads cases, runs every strategy on every case and grades which facts reach the request. The report is recorded, and a test checks that a fresh run still matches it. Success check: the recorded report matches a fresh run, the report names the case set by its SHA-256 hash, every selection stays within budget, and each strategy's known failure has a named test. You need: Python 3.11 or later and a terminal. The build uses only the standard library and calls no model.

passages.title: Compare context-selection strategies on a fixed evaluation set: Concepts
passages.text: What the grader measures Each case lists required facts: exact sentences or phrases from the conversation that a correct answer depends on. Some cases also list stale facts: earlier statements that a later turn replaced. The grader looks for each fact in the selected messages by exact text match. Fact recall is the number of required facts found divided by the number required. A complete case is one where every required fact was found. A case with a stale fact is reported separately, because a replaced decision in the request can lead to a confident wrong answer. This is a check on the request, not on an answer. It tells you what a model would be able to see. It does not call a model, and a strategy with full recall can still produce a wrong answer. Grading answers needs a model, repeated trials and a separate grader. Development and held-out splits The development split is the set of cases you look at while you write the strategies. The held-out split is kept aside and run only after the strategies are fixed. A strategy that does well on development cases but worse on held-out cases was probably shaped to the development cases.

passages.title: Compare context-selection strategies on a fixed evaluation set: Concepts
passages.text: In this build, the held-out split is not blind. The author reports writing the development cases first, using them while writing strategies.py, and writing the held-out cases afterwards, knowing the strategies and their cue list. One commit adds both splits, so the history cannot confirm that order. The cue limit matches words in two held-out cases and in neither the development cases nor the compaction build's fixture. One held-out fact, in held-pronoun, depends on it; a named test checks this. Read the held-out numbers as a second set of examples, not as an independent estimate. The report records the SHA-256 of the case set, strategies.py and counter.py, so any later change to them is visible. The four strategies Strategy Rule Origin recent Newest complete turns; stop at the first that does not fit. Context budget manager relevant Turns that share words with the question, most shared words first; skip turns that do not fit. New in this build notes Recent turns within the budget minus 64 tokens, then cue-word notes from removed turns. Context compaction hybrid The newest turn first, then relevant turns. New in this build relevant compares lowercase words after removing a short stop-word list. It does no stemming, so passwords does not match password. That is a property of this rule, not of word-overlap ranking in general.

passages.title: Compare context-selection strategies on a fixed evaluation set: Architecture
passages.text: evaluate.py runs in one Python process. It loads and validates the case set, then calls each strategy with the case and the counter. A strategy returns the selected messages; grade reads only those messages and the case's fact lists. The strategies never see the facts, so they cannot select by them. The per-case table above is the recorded result. Every case uses the same budget: tokens, with for the answer and as a margin. Most cases contain one long log turn that cannot fit. That turn is what separates the strategies: recent stops at it, and the others work around it in different ways.

The strategies Every strategy renders turns in conversation order, whatever order it chose them in. notes renders its notes exactly as the compaction build does: escaped, inside one <notes> block, after a line that says they are not instructions. recent and the recent-turn part of notes reimplement the loops from the budget and compaction builds in standard-library Python, so the comparison needs no tokenizer download. _fill adds turns in a given order and skips any turn that does not fit, which is what lets relevant and hybrid work around a long turn. passages.text: Run the tests: The suite has tests. The first runs evaluate.py and compares its output, apart from the environment block, with the recording. Others check that each split has cases, that notes uses the compaction build's escaped <notes> block, that an escaped fact still counts as found, and that the held-out notes result depends on the cue limit. The rest cover these cases: Case Expected behavior The newest turns hide an older fact behind a long turn recent keeps only the turns after the long turn and misses the fact. The question and the fact share no words relevant finds no required fact in dev-no-overlap and held-spread. A correction has no cue word notes misses the correction and includes the replaced decision. A replaced fact reaches the request The grader lists it in stale_included, separately from missing facts. A selection exceeds the budget Every strategy stays within budget on every case. A case names a fact the history never states Reject the case set. Also reject duplicate IDs, unknown splits, cases without required facts and extra fields. The case set or the code changes after recording A recorded SHA-256 hash no longer matches its file. A strategy changes the cases No strategy changes its input.

passages.title: Compare context-selection strategies on a fixed evaluation set: Failure cases
passages.text: The tests check the runner, the grader and the recorded failures. They are unit and contract checks on context selection. They are not outcome checks: no model answers a question anywhere in this build.

passages.title: Compare context-selection strategies on a fixed evaluation set: Deployment
passages.text: Run the comparison before a change ships The deployable unit here is the comparison, not a service. Run evaluate.py in your test pipeline whenever a selection strategy, its settings, the counter or the case set changes. Keep evaluation-result.json under version control, and review a change to it like a code change: which cases changed, which facts were gained or lost, which stale facts appeared. Replace the stand-in counter with your model's counter before you trust token numbers, and rerun the full set: a different counter changes what fits. Grow the case set carefully Add cases from real conversations, with personal data removed, and label their required and stale facts. Assign each new case to a split when you add it, and do not move cases between splits after you have seen results. When you change the held-out cases, the recorded hash changes and the test fails; update the recording in the same change so the review shows both. No server deployment or model call was made for this build. The tests ran on Python 3.11.11 and 3.15.0 on macOS.

passages.title: Compare context-selection strategies on a fixed evaluation set: Scaling
passages.text: Cost of the comparison The run makes one strategy call per case per strategy, and each strategy makes several counter calls. With a real tokenizer, counting dominates, as the budget build measured. This build records no timing, because the stand-in counter would not predict the cost with a real tokenizer. From fact recall to answer quality Fact recall is cheap and deterministic, which makes it a good first gate. It cannot see paraphrases, and it cannot tell whether a model uses the facts it receives. The next step is to send each selected request to a model, grade the answers against the same required facts, run several trials per case, and report failed and incomplete trials. Keep the fact-recall report beside it: when an answer is wrong, the fact-recall row shows whether the fact was missing from the request or ignored by the model.

passages.title: Compare context-selection strategies on a fixed evaluation set: Key takeaways
passages.text: - Compare strategies on one fixed case set, with the same budget, counter and grader for each. - Keep per-case results. The totals hide why a strategy failed; the cases explain it. - Report stale facts separately from missing facts: a strategy can find more facts and still send a replaced decision. - Name the limits of the grader. Fact recall measures what reaches the request, not what a model answers.

passages.title: Compare context-selection strategies on a fixed evaluation set: Best practices
passages.text: - Record the hashes of the case set and the strategy code with the results. Have someone who has not seen the strategies write the held-out cases, or say that the split is not blind. - Reject cases whose facts do not occur in the conversation, so a labeling error cannot look like a strategy failure. - Write a named test for each failure pattern you find, so a later change that fixes or breaks it shows up in review. - Do not rank strategies from a handful of synthetic cases; build a case set from your own traffic.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Problem
passages.text: Before building a RAG pipeline or an agent, follow one request all the way through. Your program starts with a string. A different process loads model weights, turns the conversation into tokens, generates an answer, and sends a response back. If those boundaries are unclear, a slow model download, a missing model and a bad answer can all look like “the AI is broken.” We will build a small Python request tracer. Give it a question and it returns three things: the exact messages and settings it sent, the model artifact it used, and the answer with token counts and timings. The question is deliberately simple: What is the capital of France? We are inspecting a request, not testing the limits of a model's knowledge. The success check is concrete: the client reaches a local server, receives a completed assistant response, records its finish reason and metrics, and can explain where failure occurred. A successful HTTP call alone is insufficient: the response can still be empty, incomplete or unsuitable for the application. Prerequisites: Python functions, dictionaries, JSON, a terminal, and the idea that an HTTP client talks to a server. No previous LangChain, ADK, PyTorch or model-training experience is needed. You will download model weights once; the Python client itself has no package dependencies.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Problem
passages.text: This build follows Programming for the builds directly: you need its Python, JSON and HTTP client lessons, nothing more. It is the first published build in Working with language models; that series' other lessons are planned. Here, the model server already supplies the HTTP boundary.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Concepts
passages.text: Your application, the server and the model have different jobs Your application decides what to ask and what to do with the response. Our application is a Python command. It creates the message list, sets an output limit, sends HTTP, checks the response and prints a trace. The model server is the running program accepting that request. This lesson uses Ollama on the same machine. It manages the model artifact and inference runtime. Keeping it local avoids a paid generation API and makes the process boundary easy to inspect. The model is the learned computation and its weights. The name in a request selects an installed artifact. It is not executable application logic, a database connection, or permission to run tools. A model tag can be updated. We record its manifest digest and pin the tested default, so an artifact change becomes visible. The runtime version and model settings matter too; the same tag alone is not a reproducibility record. Messages become a model-specific input Our request has a system message asking for one short sentence and a user message containing the question. Roles give the conversation structure. The server formats those messages for the selected model and tokenizes the result. A tokenizer maps text and control markers to token IDs. Tokens do not correspond one-for-one with words.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Concepts
passages.text: You will see 33 input tokens in our measured fixture. That includes the server's rendered input, not just the visible words in the question. Do not copy that count to another model or estimate it by splitting text on spaces. Hugging Face chat-template documentation The model is not reading your application's database. This client sends two messages on every invocation and keeps no conversation history. A later question gets earlier context only if the application includes it in a later request. Model state reused internally for speed is not an application memory contract. Input processing comes before output generation During input processing, often called prefill, the runtime processes the supplied token sequence and prepares state for generation. During decoding, it extends the sequence with output tokens. In a simple view, a token is selected, appended, and used when producing the next one. Runtimes may optimize this with batching, caching and speculative techniques; this tracer does not inspect those internals. Hugging Face prefill and decoding overview Generation ends because of a stop condition or a limit. We ask for at most 64 new tokens. The model may finish much earlier. If the server reports a length limit, treat the answer as potentially cut off even when HTTP succeeded.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Concepts
passages.text: We fix temperature to zero and a seed to reduce variation in this demonstration. That is not a guarantee of identical answers across model artifacts, runtime versions or hardware. The test suite checks the response contract; it does not require every model to write exactly “Paris.” The client can inspect the JSON it sends and the fields the server reports. It does not capture intermediate activations or independently audit the server's tokenizer. Token counts and stage timings in this lesson are server observations.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Architecture
passages.text: Two processes, one local request The client first reads the server version and installed-model metadata. It checks the selected artifact before generation. It then inspects the model template and submits one chat request. These metadata calls are separate from the timed chat call. The server has the tokenizer, template, model weights and inference runtime. The client needs none of those Python libraries. It uses only Python's standard-library HTTP and JSON modules. Follow the request through the boundary The response carries an assistant message and operational fields. Our parser accepts a completed text response, rejects empty content and tool calls, and validates the counters before presenting them. Returned text is not necessarily correct text. Application-specific answer evaluation comes later. The client makes no automatic retries. A timeout means the caller stopped waiting; it does not prove that the server stopped computing. Sending a retry immediately can duplicate work. For this first lesson, the useful behavior is a clear error and one explicit decision by the reader about what to do next.

Start the model server

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Working code
passages.text: Download the complete request-tracer source, extract it, and open its model-request directory. Install Ollama from its official download page. The measured run used Ollama 0.32.14 and Python 3.15.0; the client uses standard-library features available in Python 3.11 and later. If the Ollama app is already serving locally, use that server. Otherwise, start it in a separate terminal: In your working terminal, download the default model and make a request: Pulling downloads an artifact; it does not generate an answer. The client refuses a missing model rather than starting a hidden download during a timed request. The tested default's manifest digest is recorded in model-manifest.json and checked at startup. A mutable registry tag may later point somewhere else. If the pin fails, compare the new artifact and rerun the checks before updating it. A retained copy of the original artifact is needed to repeat that exact configuration if the registry tag moves. The archive contains source and results, not model weights. Read the complete client This is the same file supplied in the download. Start with build_request, then follow trace, fetch and parse_response in that order.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Working code
passages.text: build_request keeps the question as user-message content and fixes a small runtime context and output limit. The 4,000-character question bound limits this lesson's input size; it is not an exact token budget. Large-document context handling belongs in the context-budget manager. fetch sends one request to a loopback HTTP origin and distinguishes an HTTP failure, a connection problem, a timeout and invalid JSON. The client is intentionally local. Changing it to call a remote service also requires decisions about credentials, TLS, privacy and timeouts. trace checks the artifact identity and records a hash of the reported template. It times only the chat HTTP request. Inspecting model metadata is excluded from that timer, so it is not the entire CLI startup time. The metadata check assumes the local artifact is not changed concurrently; production model serving needs an explicit deployment/versioning contract. parse_response requires a completed assistant message with usable text. It retains the finish reason and converts nanosecond durations to milliseconds. Its generated-tokens-per-second figure covers the server's reported decoding phase only. Do not label that number end-to-end throughput. Inspect the observed response Our first run produced the following result. It required model loading and used the default question, an output limit of 64, non-streaming output and thinking disabled.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Working code
passages.text: The output limit was 64; the server reported only 3 generated tokens and a normal stop. That count need not equal the number of visible words or characters in the answer. The full trace includes the submitted messages, runtime settings, model digest and version. Run another question and inspect those fields: Predict what will change before running it. The user message should change. The system instruction should remain the same. The token counts and answer may change. Do not treat a different answer as a transport failure.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Failure cases
passages.text: Run the downloadable offline test suite: Nine test methods passed, with additional parameterized subcases. They use simulated server responses and require no weights or running model server. The separate live smoke test establishes that this client also works with the recorded local runtime and artifact. This offline test output was recorded on October 18, 2026. It checks the client contract with simulated responses; it does not run model inference. What each failure test checks Failure or boundary What the check establishes Empty, whitespace-only or oversized question Reject before making a network call. Invalid output limit Reject booleans, strings and values outside 1–256. Remote URL or invalid timeout Reject destinations outside the lesson's local-origin contract and nonfinite or negative timeouts. Model tag is absent Stop before generation; downloading is an explicit setup step. Default artifact digest changes Stop before generation under the old pin. HTTP 404, timeout or refused connection Report the failure and send no automatic retry. Invalid JSON or an error object Reject the response rather than print a fake answer. Partial response, empty assistant content, tool calls or invalid metrics Reject a response this text-only client cannot interpret. Length-limit finish Retain the finish reason so the caller can detect a potentially incomplete answer. To reproduce a real missing-model error without pulling anything:

passages.text: The command should exit with an error explaining that the tag is not installed. For a real connection failure, point the client at an unused local port: Both checks were exercised during verification. They do not cover how every model behaves on long prompts, tool requests or multimodal inputs. Those need their own contracts and fixtures.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Deployment
passages.text: This build is a local CLI plus an existing model server. There is no new FastAPI service to deploy yet. The deployment unit is the downloaded Python source and a compatible local Ollama installation with the selected model already present. For a repeatable setup, retain the source archive, the model manifest, the Ollama version, model artifact and a nonsensitive request fixture. Start the server, run the default smoke request, check its digest and finish reason, then run the offline tests. Stop the server with Ctrl+C if you launched it in a terminal. The desktop app manages its own server lifecycle. For this article's verification, Ollama used a separate loopback port and a project-local model cache. The same client ran with --base-url http://127.0.0.1:11435. Neither configuration changes the request contract. You can use the normal default port for the lesson. If moving this CLI to a Linux host, first verify that the chosen artifact and runtime fit the host's hardware. Do not expose the model server publicly as a shortcut to creating an application API. A later serving lesson adds that boundary, request controls, readiness, concurrency limits and rollback checks. This article has not deployed a VPS service.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Deployment
passages.text: The printed trace contains both input and output text. Use the supplied public question while learning. For real traffic, decide what to redact and how long to retain it before collecting traces.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Scaling
passages.text: Separate startup cost from repeated-request cost Observed on Apple M4 Pro, 48 GiB unified memory, macOS 27.0.1, Python 3.15.0 and Ollama 0.32.14, using the recorded Qwen3.5 0.8B artifact. One request ran at a time. All four requests used the same short question and settings. Observed request Client chat time Server load time Server input-processing time Server decode time First request requiring model load 1,991.71 ms 1,719.56 ms 221.90 ms 46.59 ms Warm request 1 191.95 ms 128.76 ms 30.67 ms 30.63 ms Warm request 2 174.26 ms 127.65 ms 13.30 ms 31.55 ms Warm request 3 173.58 ms 126.97 ms 13.30 ms 31.69 ms These are four observations, not capacity estimates. Repeated prefixes may be cached, the output is only three tokens, and the runtime may perform work outside the reported stage timers. Stage times should not be assumed to sum exactly to client latency. Raw results are in measured-runs.json. The useful finding is that the first request spent much of its time loading. A timeout suitable for an already-loaded model can fail during startup. Increasing it everywhere hides that difference; separating readiness/warmup from user requests makes it observable. Change one workload dimension at a time

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Scaling
passages.text: Next, measure varied prompt lengths, longer output limits and concurrent callers separately. Keep the model artifact and runtime settings fixed while changing each workload. Record queueing, failures, memory, end-to-end latency and answer quality. Do not infer multiuser capacity from the short warm-request numbers above. Longer inputs increase input-processing work and context-state requirements. Longer answers extend generation. Concurrent requests compete for resources and may be queued or batched. The exact behavior depends on the runtime and hardware; this article has not measured concurrency or the maximum context limit. Our client makes metadata calls before each generation to keep artifact identity visible. A long-running application could validate the model once at startup and revalidate when deployments change. That optimization needs a versioning rule so cached metadata cannot hide a model update. Check your understanding Before moving to the next lesson, explain these without reading the code: 1. Which process has the model weights, and which process builds the messages? 2. Why can the input count exceed the visible words in the question? 3. Why can HTTP succeed while an answer is still unusable? 4. Why is the first request slower in this measured fixture? 5. What must change if you replace the model or preserve conversation history?

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Scaling
passages.text: If you can answer those and run the tests, you have followed the system boundary this lesson set out to teach. Next is choosing a model and runtime; that lesson remains planned, so its overview lists the intended order without linking to an unfinished article.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Key takeaways
passages.text: - Your application builds the messages; the model server owns inference and the installed model artifact. - Message formatting and tokenization depend on the selected model. Visible word count is not a token budget. - A completed HTTP request can still contain empty, cut-off or incorrect output. Check the response contract and evaluate the answer separately. - Model loading, input processing and decoding contribute differently to latency. The four recorded runs describe this fixture on one machine. - A pinned model digest and recorded runtime settings make changes visible; they do not guarantee identical output across environments.

passages.title: Build a local model request tracer: Best practices
passages.text: 1. Record the actual configuration. Keep the model digest, runtime version, request settings, fixture and measured output together. 2. Bound each request. Set an output allowance and a finite timeout. Test the server's overflow behavior before accepting longer inputs; a character limit does not guarantee token fit. 3. Check finish reasons. Handle length-limited output explicitly and reject unsupported response shapes before using the answer. 4. Keep startup visible. Separate readiness and warmup from measurements of already-loaded requests. 5. Make retries deliberate. Our client sends none automatically. A timed-out request may still consume server resources. 6. Protect the trace. Use nonsensitive test questions and decide what to redact before recording real inputs and answers. 7. Verify model changes. Run the same contract tests and task fixtures for each new artifact before claiming it as a supported option.
